speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time on a point of order to seek the unanimous consent of the House with respect to a statement to be made by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) which relates to the situation of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
There have been discussions with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), with the Leader of the New Democratic Party and in turn with the financial critics and ultimately with the House Leader of each Party. The Government feels that this is a very sensitive issue in terms of the situation as it relates to the Canadian Commercial Bank. We would like to have a parliamentary opportunity at the earliest possible moment, without in any way impinging upon or negatively affecting the rights of the Opposition on an Opposition Day, to make a statement.
I have put forward a proposition to Opposition House Leaders by which a statement could be made with respect to this financial institution. I have indicated that we would be prepared to sit into the lunch hour in order to ensure that no time is lost on the Opposition Day. I will not go any further, except to say that I think it is a sensitive issue respecting a financial institution. There should be an opportunity for the Minister to address the House of Commons by way of statement and for questions, an opportunity which would not be available in Question Period. This is why we suggest this particular course of action. I am quite prepared to proceed at this time with the Minister of State for Finance or, indeed, to proceed at one o'clock this afternoon so that it will not in any
way negatively affect the Opposition Day discussion of the motion in the name of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau).
I put that proposition to the House and would like to see whether we could obtain its agreement with respect to a very important statement to be made this morning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the request of my hon. friend with respect to the desire of the Government to make a statement about the situation of the Canadian Commercial Bank. Notice of the desire of the Government to make a statement about this matter at eleven o'clock this morning reached me only about 40 minutes ago. We have been reflecting on that request. Bearing in mind the sensitivity of the situation and what the Government House Leader said about the importance of being able to put questions on the matter in a parliamentary way, it is our preference that the statement be made at the usual time at three o'clock. This would give our spokespersons a chance to review the statement in advance-we have not seen it-and to reflect upon our questions.
I point out to the House that early this morning a rather detailed press release on this was issued by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). That press release has also been the subject of news reports as early as nine o'clock this morning. I am not complaining about that; I am just saying that it is not necessary to have a statement in the House at eleven o'clock to inform either the public or the House of the situation. Therefore, under the circumstances outlined by my hon. friend with respect to the sensitivity of this situation, I think it would be most helpful to the House, in terms of the kind of response we could give to the Government statement and the kinds of questions we could ask, if we had time to reflect upon the matter until the usual time for making statements on motions at three o'clock this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, it would appear that the matter has been resolved in any event. I can well understand the position put by the House Leader of the Official Opposition. However, in the circumstances, if unanimous consent could have been sought, we certainly would not have withheld it.

I am in difficulty. The Hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) sought the floor to seek leave on a matter of unanimous consent which technically has not been granted. I find it difficult to accept any more statements on the point of order, given that the request arose under a request for unanimous consent.

That this House regrets that the Government has further postponed a budget thereby assuring that it will have gone more than eight months in office without taking any concrete action to create jobs and to establish the kind of economic confidence necessary for the realization of the hopes and aspirations of all Canadians, in particular, women, young people, farmers, fishermen, the elderly, natives and, above all, the almost one-and-one-half million unemployed.

He said: Mr. Speaker, we believe it is our duty to draw the attention of this House and of all Canadians to the incredible way the Government has been putting off the formulation of budgetary proposals in a budget speech, to inform Canadians of the direction it intends to give the economy of this country.
The Government's refusal to act has created a climate of uncertainty that is having a disastrous impact on job creation. The Conservative Government's reluctance to bring down its first budget is causing the business community to put off decisions it would otherwise have made, until it knows what the new Government's fiscal policy will be. Because of the Government's hesitation in choosing between job creation and fighting the deficit, many investment decisions have been postponed.
Mr. Speaker, this motion of censure is entirely justified. Imagine, the leader of a political party who had solutions to all the problems of this country during the election campaign not so long ago, and who had decided to wait up to eight months before bringing down his first budget! Imagine, the leader of a government who only a few months ago, last summer, was promising Canadians important fiscal measures including a complete change in oil and gas taxation what is referred to as the PGRT; removal of the tax on capital gains made by a farmer upon selling his operation; increased funding for the forestry industry, especially for reforestation . . . The same leader who proposed new taxation procedures for petro-chemi-cals, and, Mr. Speaker, you are aware of the impact of such a change, namely, abolishing the 9 per cent sales tax on gas and diesel fuel used in all primary industries; improving tax benefits for forestry workers, especially those using advanced technology; and providing tax benefits to stimulate investment in the mining industry.
Mr. Speaker, these were only a few of the 330 election promises made by the Progressive Conservative Party during the election campaign. One may well ask why the Government is unable to take four or five of these promises-and I have read a few-implement them and bring down a budget so that the business community, labour and all social partners will know what this Government's economy policy is. This kind of delay inevitably raises a certain number of questions.
The most important question of all is whether the present Government formed by the Progressive Conservative Party is still confident about the promises it made during the election campaign. The second question is, whether the delay in bringing down the Budget is due to the fact that the Government is divided and has been unable to make a choice among the contradictory promises made during the election campaign. The sincerity of their campaign promises, internal divisions all this leaves the impression that the Conservatives spent all their energy on election strategy, and, after they won, did not know what to do with their power.
This point was made very clearly by editorial writer Jeffrey Simpson in a very well researched article published in the latest issue of Saturday Night, and I shall, if I may, quote part of this text. This is what Mr. Simpson said:

What distinguished these Tories from their predecessors was their careful planning for winning an election and taking power. What they would do once in office, however, remained as much a mystery to them as to anyone else. How would they use their mandate? To what strategic ends, apart from re-election? How would they tackle the deficit, combat unemployment, improve trade relations with the United States, pursue arms reduction, raise the defence budget, entice Quebec into the Constitutional Accord, rejig social programs, reduce regional disparity and advance the status of women?
The Conservative answers to these and to many other questions were swathed in the comforting rhetoric of an election campaign whose organizational efficiency and astonishing result masked the persistent and awkward divisions in the Party.
It is not a Liberal who wrote those lines but a very senior observer of the House of Commons Press Gallery.
It is unbelievable that it will have taken eight months for a Budget to be tabled. This in itself would not be so damaging to the Canadian economy if it were not for the fact that this is a new Government. This new Government has made so many contradictory promises during the election campaign that no one knows exactly the direction it will take. Will it fight the deficit on all fronts and meet the demands of big business or will the new Government take the contrary route along with labour and social groups and fulfil the numerous promises made during the campaign? A choice must be made and this is why a new Government must present its budget in the shortest period of time possible. The new Budget becomes the framework, the orientation and the new direction.
For a Government that has promised changes, it becomes even more important that it table its first Budget as soon as possible. In the meantime, businessmen, the labour movement and social groups are in a wait and see situation. This is particularly true of those in the business community who have investment projects and want to see what the new fiscal framework will be. Is the Government going to increase taxes? If so, those new taxes may affect the profitability of business investments. Is the Government going to cut funding to the arts even more? The film producers and the artistic world told us last week about all of their problems. Will they be able to invest before knowing if other cuts will affect their particular businesses?

Mr. Speaker, putting off the first Budget until late May has serious economic implications, and we on this side of the
March 25, 1985

House fail to understand why the new Government is dragging its feet and does not unveil its economic and tax policy, what with the million and a half unemployed who are waiting for the jobs promised by the Government.
The Government gives two reasons to justify the delay: its desire to consult and the legacy of the previous administration.
The Official Opposition has nothing against consultation. The Liberal Government had also set up a consultation conference, admittedly not as elaborate as the last one. So much so that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tried last Thursday to explain the costs of his weekend conference by comparing them with those of the consultation conference convened by the former Liberal Government.
Although we are not against consultation, it must be said that the widest ranging consultation possible was held last September 4 when Quebecers as a whole voted for this Government and gave it an overwhelming majority. They voted for a Government, for a political party, for a political program. So why, after consulting the people of Canada, consult another 136 Canadians even before drafting a budget? As I said earlier, would it be that the Government does not really believe in the policies it proposed to the people of Canada? If only the Government had seen the weekend economic summit as a golden opportunity to table three or four policy papers to explain the various components of the problem confronting the nation and to propose hypothetical solutions, three or four policy guidelines, and then sought the advice of those leaders to know which policy would most likely produce a genuine solution to the problem! No, the Government chose to remain uncommitted.
As expected, there was something for everybody. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) found himself in agreement with those who advocate higher budget expenditures and others who strongly support a lower deficit. The only participant who nearly got rapped on the knuckles was one who dared voice mildly critical remarks against our Prime Minister's pal, President Reagan of the United States.
In fact, the only real issue on which consensus was reached-and I think the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) will agree with me-was the petition signed by 87 people urging the withdrawal of the unemployment insurance program amendments because they affect too many Canadians. I say without reservation that the summit conference was first and foremost an exercise in public relations. Most observers on Parliament Hill in Ottawa agree that the Mulroney Government operates on the basis of opinion polls.

Yet the Mulroney Government is a Government which is prepared to take action only according to the polls. For the Prime Minister, that is what really counts.

Allan Gregg, President of Decima Research, the pollster of the Progressive Conservative Party, is more important than the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) or any other member of the Cabinet. What does Allan Gregg say about consultation? I would like to quote Mr. Gregg as he was reported in the Saturday Night magazine. He said:
We interviewed groups until they were coming out of our ears ... but there is no consensus on what should be done. We are at point "A" and people sense we should get to point "C" but there is no agreement on point "B". The people have bought the Conservative agenda but not the Conservative philosophy.
That is what the pollster for the Progressive Conservative Party said. Sure, Mr. Gregg is more important than the Minister of Finance and many other members of the Cabinet! What does Mr. Gregg say about the consultation process? In the same article he went on to say:
-the consultative process would allow the Government to share the blame if results did not match expectations.
He continued:
"The Government certainly hopes it can bring people around through public education", said Gregg, "and Mulroney praises himself of being able to get people to do things his way. But if he fails, the Government will be able to share responsibility".
What Mr. Gregg has said is that it is more important to follow the polls than to follow the advice of the Minister of Finance. For those who do not want to hear, there is nothing we can do. But for those who want to understand, and for those who want to read the facts and accept that two plus two equals four, the whole exercise of the Ottawa summit was to use the Canadian television network so that the Prime Minister of Canada could share the blame of his failure if the Budget does not work, and keep all the praise for himself if it succeeds.
I would say that the whole process of the Ottawa summit conference during the weekend was a public relations exercise for the Conservative Party and the Prime Minister. The summit was designed as a tool to make other people share the blame for the failures of the Government. The summit and the consultation process were invented by the pollster of the Conservative Party, using Canadian taxpayers' money, to fulfil a partisan objective. All those who participated in good faith at the summit will realize sooner rather than later that they were used for partisan purposes.
As I previously stated, there was only one example of consensus at the summit. That was the petition which was signed by 87 participants asking that the changes presented by the Mulroney Government to the unemployment insurance program be revised, because as designed it would affect too many beneficiaries.

Mr. Speaker, the second reason which was given to explain the delay in bringing down a budget is the financial mess handed down by the Liberal Government. Let us see what does this legacy involve. I shall try to provide a few indications from a paper tabled by the Minister of Finance, and I imagine that these figures will not be questioned as they are those of the Conservative Government itself.

Let us look first at the general economic growth. In 1984, the Domestic National Product increased at a rate of 4.7 per cent. Mr. Speaker, this was the best performance of the Canadian economy since 1976. Still referring to the same document, if we compare the growth of the Canadian economy to that of the member countries of the Summit, in other words, the major industrialized countries, we find that our rate of growth was third in the world in 1984 and second in 1983, right after that of the United States. Mr. Speaker, that kind of financial situation is not really that bad!
In the field of employment, always according to the figures contained in this paper, we find that the number of jobs increased by 2.5 per cent in 1984. If we compare Canada's performance to that of the major industrialized countries, according to the figures of the Department of Finance, we were second in the world, immediately after the United States, and in 1983, we were third.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives can complain all they want, but being in second and third place among all industrialized countries with regard to job creation is not that bad in my humble opinion.
If we look at what happened in the employment sector during the period immediately preceding the election of this Government, we find that, in 1984, the Canadian economy produced 108,000 new jobs during the second quarter, 67,000 in the third quarter and 88,000 in the last quarter. Once more, as the Canadian economy had just been through one of the worst economic crises in the history of the Western world after the crisis of the thirties, it seems to me that a quarterly average of 87,000 new jobs created just before the coming to power of this Government is not that bad a legacy either.
If we look at the level of inflation, we see that, thanks to the 6 and 5 policy, Canada had a remarkable performance which compares quite well with that of other industrialized countries. In addition, when this Government took over, the rate of inflation was about 3.4 per cent, one of its lowest levels ever. Once more, Mr. Speaker, this is not such a bad legacy.
There is also the trade balance and the record surpluses in the trade balance of over $20 billion in 1983 and 1984. I could refer to other economic sectors, such as foreign investment, to show that the performance of the former Liberal Government did not represent such a terrible legacy. On the other hand, I understand that it can be useful in the short term to distort the facts to try to gain a few points in the polls, but while this can be useful in the short term, in the long term, it creates a false image of our country and this discourages Canadian and foreign investments.
Mr. Speaker, we do have a major problem that should be solved, and that is the deficit. However, before they blame the former Government, I would like the Conservative Members and the Minister of Finance to tell us what they would have
done in 1982 when we were going through one of the worst economic crises ever without increasing the deficit. Would the Minister of Finance have withdrawn from under the unemployed our social security net which took years to develop? Would the Minister of Finance have refused to implement job creation programs simply to avoid a deficit, he who has just approved budgets when we are in a period of economic recovery? I suggest that the deficit theory preached by the Minister of Finance is generally valid, but it becomes unappropriate in a larger context and over a longer period. In addition, when these people try to prove that the deficit we have in 1985 is due only to external factors, they forget that we had an economic crisis in 1982.
Those people who are now criticizing and saying that it is because of the financial situation they inherited that they cannot introduce a budget, where were they last summer? Why did they go around the country making promises which, according to certain Members of the present Cabinet, would cost $20 billion? Mr. Speaker, there are certain facts which should be underlined. Since this Government had answers and proposed a change only a few months ago during the election campaign, this is the question I ask now: why wait eight months. This is unheard of because in the meantime life goes on. And looking back at the week-end conference we see that the business community was in favour of lowering the deficit while social groups and labour said this was no top priority. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, depending on the direction that will be taken now, what is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) liable to choose, employment or the deficit? This will have an impact on taxation. This will affect consumer purchasing power, and it is my view, Mr. Speaker, that such a delay in bringing down a Budget will be bad for the over-all Canadian economy. We, of the Official Opposition, want to have that major failure brought to the attention of the public.

speechtext: Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, by analyzing the figures for the month of January, the Hon. Member will appreciate that for every dollar this country spent it had to borrow 36 cents. In other words, it took in only 64 cents in taxes for each dollar spent. Even if we had full employment, everyone in the country working flat out, we would still have a massive deficit.
That clearly points out the need for a tremendous amount of consultation among all groups in the country so that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) can come up with new and different methods of handling the problems. Although the consultation will have taken some eight months by May, surely that is not a great length of time, particularly when we did have on November 8 a rather comprehensive financial statement. A Budget means change and surely before changes are made there should be consultation with all of the players in the
March 25, 1985

economy, particularly in view of the massive amount of fiscal problems the country faces.
Is there something wrong with consultation? Is there something wrong with trying to get some sort of consensus as to how we should proceed with the problems? This is a problem for everyone.

Mr. Speaker, I said in my speech that there is nothing wrong with consultation. But I also said that we in this country had the largest consultation process that anyone can have, and that was the election. We had that consultation and you, ladies and gentlemen, have been elected on promises you made. We now need action. That is the point of view expressed in this motion. After the largest consultation anyone can have through the election, more consultation now is not a substitute for action. What we need is action now.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague for his most interesting and substantive speech. I have a few questions that I want to ask. In view of the delay by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in bringing down a Budget, in view of those nine months of dilly-dallying, in view of the commitment to create jobs, jobs and more jobs, could the Hon. Member tell me if, in researching the subject, he has compared budget tablings over the previous years to see whether there had been such lengthy delays in Canada before? And second, could he comment on the Government boasting that they have created 100,000 jobs since they came to power on September 4? Could he tell me how they compare with the previous administration, let us say in recent years?

Obviously, Mr. Speaker, I did not introduce this motion without having done some research, because if recent history had shown that most new governments after coming to power had waited eight or nine months, there would be a tradition which certainly would not justify a motion such as this one. Indeed I researched that, and I found out that when a Liberal government-1 did not go as far back as the early days of Confederation but to the early 60's-
Even if we except Mr. John Diefenbaker's election on June 10, 1957, which was almost immediately followed by another general election in which Mr. Diefenbaker obtained a large Conservative majority, there was a two month delay between the election and the tabling of the budget. When the Liberal Party was elected in 1963, the budget came two months and five days after the election of a new government.
Withdrawn right after!

When on June 25, 1968, a new government was elected, the budget followed four months after the election of that new Prime Minister. On May 22, 1979, I think there was a government that was elected under Mr. Joe Clark, and

the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) only waited six months before tabling his budget. Maybe the Minister's comment might be more appropriate in this instance. In 1980, after the Liberals came back to power, a budget followed two months later. But now eight months have gone by, or close to nine. The election took place on September 4, and if a budget is brought down on May 21st, eight months and 12 days will have elapsed.
Now, with respect to jobs, which was the second part of the question, the Government is bragging about having created 100,000 jobs during the First six months of its administration. Now, 1 am not sure how the month of September could be accounted for since the transfer of powers occurred half way through that month. So taking September on each side to be fair to everyone during the six months previous to the transfer of powers to the Conservative Government, 175,000 jobs were created, and during the first six months of the Tory administration, the number declined by 75,000.

Mr. Speaker, with reference to the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), could he explain to me why the Canadian people voted in droves against the previous government, if not because of its poor economic performance?

Mr. Speaker, I am quite surprised to hear the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin) ask this question. We have indicated on several occasions that you have been elected, gentlemen, because the Canadian people believed you when you assured them that you could reduce the deficit while fulfilling some $20 billion worth of election promises.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: A little while ago, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) dealt at length with the late introduction of the budget and quoted a few figures. It has clearly been established that the budget is a little late in coming; during the election campaign, however, the Canadian people heard a great many PC candidates speak about the new approach and direction which were to give investors renewed confidence; yet, as the recovery seems rather slow, in spite of a new government which claimed it could foster confidence and start the economy moving again, I wonder what could be the effects-perhaps the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides who has a financial background could tell us-of a long delay in introducing the budget on investors' decision to go ahead and invest to create new jobs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans).
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I take the hon. gentlemen with me wherever I go. Some places I go I need them, I can tell you! I always wonder just what one is supposed to do while waiting for the overwhelming applause to die down. I have never quite made up my mind what it is. However, I do thank them both very much.
On a more serious note, which I am sure you would have expected me to arrive at quickly in any event, I would like to say that this is certainly an omnibus resolution. It does cover the waterfront and sets out in some detail the concerns that a large number of people across Canada feel about the inaction of the present Conservative Government. As I read it, it reminds me a lot of the resolution which I introduced in 1982 when the Liberal Government was in office. I recall that at that point we were concerned about the Government's inaction with regard to jobs. We were concerned about the Government's inability to come to grips with the problems of the farming community and its inability to come forward with policies which would adequately deal with the fishermen of Canada. I am sure you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that on that very day we were discussing the plight of the elderly and the problem of natives in Canada. In fact, this resolution could well have been addressed to the previous Government with the same degree of validity. It would have been very valid.
As I read the resolution I was thinking of the events leading up to last September 4. As the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) travelled across Canada he berated the Liberals,
and justifiably so, for the way they handled the high office of government. I can remember watching with interest as the present Prime Minister laid out the problems of Canada and led people to believe that he had some solutions at hand which could be introduced to attempt to resolve those problems. I admit that he was vague. As I look back now I can well understand why. I admit that he did not put forward concrete suggestions. Looking back now I can well understand why.
I remember his saying that one of the problems of the Government was that it had lost the confidence of Canadians. He said that the actions of the Government in terms of dealing with the unemployed, dealing with the imbalances between the various regions in Canada and with regard to setting up a new arrangement for supporters by way of patronage were unsatisfactory, unacceptable, and must be changed.
I am sure it will go down in history when the present Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), embarrassed as he was over the legacy that had been left to him by way of political patronage appointments, was attempting to explain that he had had no option in that regard. He said that he had been informed that if he did not make the appointments he would not have a sufficient number of Members to carry on in government and he therefore simply had to do as the previous Prime Minister indicated he must and make the appointments in the way that he did. In what was perhaps his finest moment, the former Leader of the Opposition leaned forward, reached out as he does, and said to the now Leader of the Official Opposition: "Sir, you had an option. You could have said no."
It is amazing what a short passage of time will do for a person's sensibilities in that regard. It is amazing how the Prime Minister seems to have forgotten what it was that caused the deterioration of the Liberal Government in office. The cause was that they were unable, or maybe unwilling, to deal with the real problems of Canada.
When the Government of today sought office it left the impression that it had an over-all plan for dealing with the serious problem of unemployment. I recall the same Prime Minister saying that after he was elected the first priority would be jobs, jobs, jobs. He said it in the House of Commons and out of the House of Commons. He indicated that it would be his priority and he left the impression that he had some views as to how that particular difficult situation could be resolved.
We have waited. Six and one-half months have now passed and there has still not been a single, solitary, concrete proposal on how to deal with the problems of the 1.5 million plus people who are still unemployed. There are 1.5 million people registered for employment, but in actual fact we all know that there are another 100,000, 200,000, or maybe even more, who have long since given up. They have decided that it does not make sense any more and they will therefore go about the rest of their lives without seeking gainful employment. They did not come by that decision easily. They came by that decision because they were forced to it. Circumstances quite clearly acted against their being able to find employment.
March 25, 1985

The Government misled them in September and October by leaving the impression that somehow it would be able to bring forward programs which would improve the opportunities for employment across Canada. The Government has had ample time to do it. There can be no excuse for a Government which cannot come forward within seven months with legislation to put in place the programs that it used as the basis for an electoral platform. There is an obligation on those who seek office, not only to tell the public of Canada what they stand for, but also, if they are successful, to follow through with the things which they themselves advanced as being the reasons why they should be elected.
The Government cannot substitute consultation for action. I watch with interest as the Prime Minister, in carefully staged performances, appears before the media and sets out how he is trying to get the advice of everyone, how he will take those positions, which are poles apart, and find a way to meld them together into something called a national policy for economic recovery.
Hear, hear!

One of the Conservative back-benchers says "hear, hear". I put it to the Hon. Member that it is impossible to take the views of the groups in society that are polarized and find a compromise. What we must do is choose a direction for the country and then produce the legislative proposals that will bring that direction into reality. This Government has failed to do that.
I walked down the streets of Stratford on the weekend. I was asked how the local Member for Stratford was doing. I said that no doubt he was doing fine. I spoke to people from a variety of walks of life and areas in the immediately surrounding Stratford community. Their reaction was quite simple. I asked them what they thought of the new Government. They said: "Well, the Government is certainly taking its time." I asked whether things were better now than they were before. Their reaction was that things had not changed, that there had been no improvement. Those who were unemployed prior to September last year remain unemployed. Those who had difficulty maintaining their family farms were still having difficulty maintaining their family farms. As they talked about the planting season they found that they were having difficulty even now getting the necessary capital to purchase seed, to purchase the necessary fertilizers in order to get on with the job. That was exactly the situation in which they found themselves at this same time in 1984, they told me. I asked small business people whether they were finding it any easier than a year ago. I asked them whether things were improving any. Without exception they told me that this will probably be one of the worst years they have had in the last five.
The policy of the Government is a non-policy at the moment. The sense the Government has tried to leave is that somehow or other there would be an immediate improvement because somehow Conservatives exude confidence, that out of

that confidence comes action and out of that action comes benefit, and that that had not yet taken hold. In Stratford I came to the conclusion that if things were bad in 1984, as they were, things were equally as bad in 1985.
I then spoke to people in my own home community. I talked to them about how things were going there. What did I discover, Mr. Speaker? I discovered that there are now fewer people working in the area than there were a year ago, that the over-all economic conditions had not improved, that the opportunities available a year ago are not as plentiful as they were then, and that we have 2,500 people who were previously employed in the Steel Company of Canada and who remain unemployed. We still have upwards of 50 per cent of the construction industry unemployed. We have plants that have announced in the last few months that they will be closing and moving away. The most recent one, as my colleague says to me, John Inglis, a matter which 1 raised in the House of Commons, is a plant that was given $2 million or $3 million by the previous administration for the purpose of purchasing Admiral Corporation. Having purchased it, having sold the assets, and having had the most profitable year in history, it then turned around and is closing down the plant that was the basic manufacturing plant for its entire chain in Canada. That will be closed down and five or six hundred people and their families will not be able to find employment.
I say to the Government, why not make it a condition of providing public funds that companies must at least maintain employment levels? But the Government cannot do that, that is interfering with the private sector.
Later today we will be dealing with a problem that has arisen over the course of the last few weeks when a bank, mismanaged perhaps, will go under unless we give it assistance. The Government will, as it normally does in those circumstances, dash forward and offer aid. It shows the difference in the attitude of the Government but what happens when a person owes a mortgage to a bank, or perhaps a farmer owes a mortgage to a bank? What happens when we say to the Government: "Don't you think in the long-term best interests of the community that that person should be sustained?" The Government's answer is that it can do nothing about it. That is the private system. If a person is unfortunate enough to manage his or her affairs in such a way that that person cannot sustain himself, then it is just too bad. But when a bank manages its affairs in such a way as to place itself in jeopardy, the first thing that happens is that we are inundated with requests to save the bank from itself.
That is a double standard and we have to look at that very seriously. We will debate that later; I do not want to get into the details of it at the moment. There is a serious double standard in this country when it comes to the larger corporate entities. The Government seems willing, maybe even a little reluctant, to proceed with bail-outs of all different kinds, but when it comes to the private individual affected by the same kind of decision-making, there does not seem to be any assistance for them.

This leads me to a group in society who have been hardest hit, in my opinion, by the most recent economic conditions. This is a group which desperately cries out for assistance, a group that has to be treated differently from all others inasmuch as this group's circumstances are different from everyone else's. I am talking about people who fall between their early 50s and into their 60s. These are people who have worked all their lives and on whose backs and with whose sweat this country was built. Generally speaking they have rarely ever drawn a day of unemployment insurance in their lives. They have worked with industries, many of them at lower paying jobs without substantial benefits available to them. I have been pleading on behalf of those people for years with the previous administration and with this administration. I look at the Minister of Finance and I say to him that there is an absolutely desperate need for policy directed at those individuals in our society. It is unfair that those people, after having worked for all of their working lives, many of them starting in their early teens, should end up at age 55, 56, or 57 faced with the prospect of not being able to find employment, faced with the prospect of not being able to contribute to pension plans and faced with the prospect of not being part of the Canada Pension Plan and contributing during their normal last 10 years of work. Those people will lose not only in the short run because of the disastrous consequences of non-governmental action on the economic front, but they will lose in the long run because they will not be able to secure for themselves and their families the kind of economic and financial security that they had reasonably expected would be afforded to them.
I say to the Government that it did not require an economic conference across the street to come to the conclusion that there was that group in society who simply have to have action and have it now. Neither did it require a conference across the street to discover that small-business people are unable to afford to pay the exorbitant interest rates that Rowland Frazee and others like him charge on behalf of the banks. I could not help but feel ill when I watched Mr. Frazee on television saying that the big problem in our society is the size of the deficit.
Let me tell Hon. Members something. Where was Mr. Frazee when interest rates were rising, rising and rising, and continuing to contribute significantly to the over-all deficit requirements of Canada?

Why was the minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) not asking Mr. Frazee that question when he used to mouth off on this side of the House when he was the critic for finance? Where is the Government telling the banks it is time the banks lived up to their responsibilities?

The only difference between the Hon. Minister of Justice and myself is that I mean what I say.

The problem with the Conservative Government is that when its members were in opposition they said all the right things. Now all we get is silence. The Minister of Justice used to stand and rail against the banks and high interest rates. Now that he is in government, he has been immediately silenced. We never hear a word from him. In fact, I think he has been muzzled. The only time he ever speaks is when he is sitting in his place. He is not allowed to rise to make a speech or a statement, for fear he will embarrass the Government. Many of us who are here remember how the Tories in opposition talked about the need for assistance for farmers and small business people and for relief from high interest rates. Where are the programs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You just open your big gap of a mouth, that is all.
We all know that the Minister of Justice, voluminous though he is in his-

Keep going.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If you irritate me, I will make a speech and demolish you.

All I can say, since my time is up, is that I would be willing to yield to the Hon. Minister of Justice. On every occasion which we have appeared publicly, I have yet to be demolished. I would be happy to have him rise.
In closing, we support the intent of the motion. It is quite clear that the Government was elected without having developed policy to meet the needs of Canadians. The process through which it is going now is one of dividing the community rather than finding an honest consensus. The Government is creating division rather than working toward bringing forward programs to meet needs. This Government in fact is a fraud.

Mr. Speaker, I am always interested in the comments of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), because he indicates that he knows what he means, that what he says is true, and so on. Does he really believe that it is not good for Canada to have Bob White in the same room with Rowland Frazee? Does he really think that we should not have consultation with organized labour, the big banks and big industries? Does he really think that consumer groups and others should not be talking together? Is that the kind of government that he would have us run, the kind of government

March 25, 1985

we had before? Does he want a confrontational government, or does he want a government which attempts to obtain ideas and input from all sides of the community? Is there anything wrong with getting input from other people?
No, no.
Why are you against it, then?
I was going to tell you, if you would listen.
We are listening.
Are you really?
Intently.
Wonderful.
I am hanging on to every word.

Good. Let me say to the Hon. Member who asked the question that there is nothing wrong with consultation, but consultation is not a substitute for action. When the Government of today was elected in 1984, its members had left the impression with the public of Canada that not only had they identified the problems, but that they had solutions. They asked for support on the basis of being able to put forward a new agenda for Canada, an agenda which would include solutions to the problems which they had identified when they were in opposition.
It does not require ongoing consultation in advance of the introduction of preliminary solutions. The Government's obligation is to bring forward its proposals so that they can be debated by those people who attended the conference and by the House of Commons. Then it should proceed with whatever consensus develops as a result of the debate. If it goes out and seeks consensus for the next four years, we will be in the same position as the one in which we are today, come the next election.

Mr. Speaker, does the Hon. Member not think that the arrangements with the United States to lessen trade problems are progress? I am referring, for example, to those arrangements in the steel industry, about which he is talking all the time; those in the softwood industry; those on the east and west coasts in terms of a salmon treaty; and those with respect to acid rain. Are not those kinds of things real progress? Is that not real decision-making? Why does he not stand in his place and congratulate the Government for getting down to business and doing things which have not been done for years and years?

I would be willing to congratulate the Government for doing things which have not been done for years, but unfortunately I have difficulty identifying with those things. What worries me about the examples used by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is that in fact the tendency of the Government to try to work out arrangements with the President of the United States does not in itself

result in a change in U.S. policy. In part the problems rest with the White House, but the decision on whether or not
Do you not think they are progress?

Let me finish. The decision on whether or not there will be an easing of trade relations with the U.S. rests in the Congress and in the Senate. At the very time the President of the United States was speaking with our Prime Minister in Quebec City, Senators and Congressmen were moving forward with restrictive legislation to keep Canadian-made products out of the United States. There was ongoing nonsense dialogue with the President wherein somehow or other he said: "Brian, we will do our best. We will see what we can do. We will keep it in mind. I will have a committee study it. I will refer it to someone else". The President does not have the power to change the problem areas which have been irritants over the last few years. It would only be because of our ability to reach the Senate and the Congress that we would be able to change most of the irritants.
The Hon. Member knows as well as I do that we asked the Prime Minister to raise with the President the whole question of sugar quotas, the quotas on sugar-based products, and the difficulties they were causing for Canadian companies and therefore Canadian workers. What did the President do in that regard? Prior to coming to Canada he imposed global quotas which effectively cut off the sale of products manufactured in Canada which contained a particular percentage of sugar or sugar substitute. We said that was unfair. Why was it unfair? First, because it was done without consultation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Consultation first!

It was done without any consultation with Canada and, second, without any reference to the International Trade Commission. We suggested that that was the appropriate way to follow. That was the agreement we had with the United States. The President did not even follow the agreement. Then when we asked whether something could be done about it, what did the Prime Minister do? He said that he would go back and talk with him about it. In the meantime, unless action is taken now many of those companies will not only be locked out of the U.S. market for now but will be locked out forever. If they do not get their products on the shelves before October this year, the chance of them being able to build up consumer and customer acceptance is severely restricted. The end result will be that we will lose that market entirely and lose those jobs. The entire discussion between Canada and the United States is a sham at the moment. We are trying to find ways to improve the relationship, and the Congress and the Senate of the United States are doing everything in their power to provide further protection.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The period for questions and comments is over. We will resume debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak on the motion of the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), who is not here anymore. It gives me an excellent opportunity to discuss some of the accomplishments of this Government over the period of time that we have been in office, to address the financial and economic problems that we were presented with as a new Government.
I am delighted that the Hon. Member's Party is finally waking up to the needs of the people who are set out in this motion, the young people, women, farmers, fishermen, the elderly and the natives. For a number of years in power they ignored the needs of those people. That is why we have been left with the disastrous economic situation that was presented to us on September 4. It is about time the Members opposite started to think about the people in this country and not solely about their existence as a political Party.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we are concerned about Canadians, and the various people in our society who have been seriously affected by the economic problems. We have presented a most comprehensive economic strategy. The framework that was set out on November 8 for our economic and financial policies was, I think, regarded by most people as one of the most comprehensive policy statements that has ever been set out by a particular Government.
This was an agenda for change, the change that Canadians asked for by their votes on September 4.
It is a comprehensive and very realistic exercise. It responded very clearly to the needs of the country and the needs of Canadians. It is a very sensible approach to government. It is a new approach though, a new approach that calls for consultation and co-operation among the different elements of society and the different regions of the country. We intend during the course of this exercise to protect the citizens who have been affected and to build economic growth, build job creation so we can address clearly the problems with which we have been faced.
Are we delaying unduly? According to many Members opposite, the November 8 statement was referred to as a Budget. They said: "It's a Budget, why can't we have a Budget debate?" Now they are saying they have not had a Budget. The reason they said it was a Budget last November was that it was so comprehensive and far-reaching in its impact on Canadians. I realize that it has the importance of a Budget because of the extensive nature of that statement. However, Hon. Members cannot have it both ways.
The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides said that we have been delaying too long with our Budget. Let me remind him that in 1980, after only nine months out of power, Mr. Mac-Eachen, the then Minister of Finance, took about the same amount of time to present a new Budget, a Budget that was a disaster. The second Budget was also a disaster which left him out of office very, very quickly.
We will wait to see how well the Canadian people are going to respond to the Budget that 1 will be putting forward during the week of May 20. Hon. Members should recognize that we are approaching this Budget in a way that will get it right and get it right the first time, not fumble away like previous Ministers of Finance and Liberal Governments have done with Budget after Budget which did not address the problems. In fact, they compounded the problems they were faced with at that time.
The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) said that consultation is no substitute for action. He is right. I say that because we have acted in a number of ways and I would like to set them out. We said we would deal with the deficit and we did by cutting expenditures by $4.2 billion in the November 8 statement. We reduced the projected level of spending for this year and are committed to continue to do so throughout the life of this Parliament. We have also acted in putting an additional $1 billion into job-creation programs, linked with training so that those job-creation programs will be career development jobs, not short-term, dead-end jobs, as was the policy of the previous Government. We have moved in the area of social assistance, increasing the spouse's allowance to 85,000 low-income Canadians, mainly women. We announced and implemented a fuel tax rebate of three cents per litre on motor fuels used off highway by farmers, fishermen and other primary producers.
March 25, 1985

Other actions that we have introduced during this period of time have addressed clearly the greatest need of the greatest number of Canadians. I want to refer to some of these as well. However, let me say that Opposition Members and other Members have focused only on the deficit itself. They have ignored the far-reaching nature of other elements of our economic policy as set out in the November 8 statement. We said that the private sector must be given the opportunity to grow. How have we done that? We said that there are government-created obstacles to growth and there is a need for a greater degree of incentive in areas such as research and development, trade, investment and the training of our people.
Let me get back to government intervention. Over the years we have seen Governments develop an intricate web of regulations, subsidies and other forms of intervention which have slowed down the private sector. This we are committed to remove and we have set out a clear game plan as to how we are going to remove it.
Let us look at some of the actions we have taken along those lines. Investment Canada-removing the greatest obstacle that has been in place to foreign investment. With regard to the National Energy Program, my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), is very close to an agreement which will remove the taxation and regulatory impediments to a very, very powerful industry in this country.
The Atlantic Accord on energy development was a great step forward in freeing up the resources of the private sector and in developing the energy reserves off the coast of Newfoundland. The Regional Development Agreement with Quebec was the first since 1974 that any Government has signed with the Province of Quebec, along with the subagreements in the areas of communication, tourism and industrial development.
There is simply no truth that this Government has not been acting. Last weekend there was the National Economic Conference. A few weeks back the First Ministers met. Those are clear steps forward in drawing together the Canadian family to develop the ideas that are necessary, to address the economic problems that we all face. We are all in this together. We saw 135 people last weekend sitting around that conference table trying to understand the position of the other side and putting forward ideas as to how we can address the problems. Canadians can adapt and are willing to adapt, but they have to know what the problems of the other persons are because that is their nature. That is how we can get economic renewal.
It was a sign of desperation on the part of Members opposite when they were reduced to the ritual game-playing over the timing of a Budget. It was a childish response on Friday afternoon because Members opposite wanted to have the afternoon off to go home. They tried to deflect the attention of Canadians. The Hon. Member opposite has had to work because she was at the Economic Conference. I think she learned something. All of her game-playing colleagues went home for the weekend. They took the afternoon off.

Members opposite are trying to deflect attention away from the National Economic Conference by saying that it is a sham and that it did not produce anything. Hon. Members opposite are out of touch with Canadians. They are out of touch with the people who were at that conference. They should say to the people who were at that conference that it was only a public relations exercise and was not worth their time. I think Members opposite would find that there would be a great deal of disagreement with that from the labour people, the management people, the people from the arts community, the people from the women's groups and the people from the disabled groups. All the people to whom I spoke felt it was a very worth-while exercise which did accomplish an awful lot of things. We on this side of the House as well as many Canadians feel that we welcome opportunities to discuss these views together in order to understand the views of other Canadians, because that will help in our decision making.
I would like to deal with the part of the motion which deals particularly with confidence in the economy. I think that the Hon. Member is trying to cast a pall over the things that are happening in the market-place, in the economy and in the real world because Members opposite do not like what they see out there. They are worried about what is happening. Canadians are ignoring the Opposition for this reason. Canadians see the Opposition as being irrelevant. The polls, the National Economic Conference and the economic statistics are saying that self-confidence and confidence in the Government is growing.
I would like to quote from an article in today's La Presse. [Translation]
In an editorial in La Presse I read the following, and I quote:
Which means that Mr. Mulroney's team, after six months in power, has managed to win the confidence of all regions and all groups, thereby raising almost unreasonable expectations. There is a caveat there for Budget Day.

Confidence is a vital ingredient but let us look at what is happening. I would like to talk about some economic statistics that underline the fact that confidence is returning to the country. Recently there has been a real scramble among economists to upgrade their figures. This has happened since we came into power. Many economists have upgraded their figures by one-half of 1 per cent in real growth for this year. A survey done by the Purchasing Management Association of Canada shows that production in the manufacturing sector is growing strongly and that shipments in new orders are increasing at double-digit rates at the current time. The survey also showed that employment and new orders are on the increase. Statistics Canada has said that investment in the manufacturing sector is expected to increase by 26 per cent for this year and that the oil and gas drilling industry is up by 20 per cent. This is a very important statistic which affects not only western Canada but all parts of Canada because of the many suppliers to that industry. We have made a good start by indicating to the industry that we understand its problems and

March 25, 1985
Supply
it is responding with its investment dollars and creating jobs as it does so.
There are other statistics as well. Manpower Temporary Services say that there is an encouraging improvement in the outlook for job openings in the second quarter and that that optimism is shared by employers right across the country.
Canadians made a very important change on September 4. They made a change that brought a fundamental improvement to the national outlook. A recent survey showed that Canadians expressed confidence in the handling of unemployment now relative to what they were saying a year earlier. The unemployment rate has gone down from 11.6 per cent to 11 per cent. That is progress. In fact, 84,000 jobs have been created since September. We can do better than that, we should do better than that, but it is a good start.
We have made a good start as well at controlling inflation. We are doing better than the United States in that area. We are moving in a positive direction. There have been no miracles but there has been solid evidence of growth and an improvement in confidence. We need more but we have made satisfactory progress. Canadians are too realistic to expect miracles or to expect a quick fix to happen overnight. However, they know that the fundamental problems are being addressed and that we are dealing with those problems we inherited.
Let us look at the real world. Economists have noted that consumer borrowing has been increasing strongly in recent months. That shows confidence in the future. Canadians are talking with their actions. What consumers are actually doing is indicated by how much money they are borrowing and where it is being spent. Retail sales were 12 per cent higher in January than they were a year earlier. That is a very respectable increase even after the effects of inflation are taken into account.
There is no doom and gloom out there, Mr. Speaker. The doom and gloom is right here with Members opposite. They are walking around with a little cloud over their heads. They do not want to come out from under that cloud. They do not want to face the real world.
I would like to touch on some of the criticisms that have been made by some Hon. Members regarding the consensusbuilding process. I do not understand it. I simply do not understand why Members opposite say that this is a waste of time. Hon. Members should have listened to Prime Minister Hawke, the head of the Australian Labour Party, because he shares some of the political viewpoints of the two opposition Parties. Surely his words demonstrate the importance of consensus. His message to us was that consultation leads to better understanding, better understanding leads to more cooperation and more co-operation clearly leads to economic growth. That is an excellent example from another country, a country not dissimilar to Canada, demonstrating that we are on the right track in moving toward a great degree of consensus.
1 do not understand why Members opposite are so negative. I say they are out of touch with the Canadian people. Only last week some Members from across the floor were suggesting that the Government tell delegates to the National Economic
Conference to go home. They mocked the Government and said that the Government had already made up its mind. I indicated very clearly by saying that the Budget would be like that we have not made up our minds but are listening and are open to the good suggestions that are coming forward.
I would like to touch on the consensus that was reached at the National Economic Conference last weekend. Consensus was reached on the importance of the problems of unemployment, interest rates and the deficit but consensus was also reached that we must be very sensitive to the regional considerations and to the impact of our actions on the handicapped, youth, native people and workers. We must be careful that we do not affect workers unduly by the decisions that we might make when dealing with the deficit. There was not a full consensus on this point, but a number of people from the labour side as well from other communities said to us that the deficit is a problem with which we must deal because it is too high. They said that they might have some different priorities but that it is a problem with which we must deal.
Training and retraining should receive top consideration by the Government in order to deal with the effects of technological change. We talked about some of the ways in which we could do this. Business representatives agreed that business should be prepared to pull back from the public trough. That was stated very clearly by business representatives. Government, labour and management all agreed that we must coordinate our efforts in dealing with technological changes and their effect on people and people's ability to adapt to technological change. Only through consultation will we be able to address that problem in a satisfactory way. There was full agreement that we must look carefully at access to capital by small business, the visible minorities and women. We must be willing to discuss incentives within this context.
I am sure that it is difficult for Hon. Members to appreciate that the Government is not trying to fool anyone. We have placed our agenda on the table. It is there for all to see. That is why we are getting such a good response on this consultative effort. People know what we want to address and they are coming to us with a great many very useful ideas. The National Economic Conference was the most comprehensive assembly of Canadians ever to discuss with a national Government the problems which we all face. Very positive attitudes and contributions came forward from all participants.
Canadians are not confused by what the Government is doing. They are insisting that they want to be a part of the process. Not only are they telling the Government that they want that, but they are showing it by their actions and the clear confidence which they are expressing in this Government. This Party has the confidence of Canadians. Canadians have understood the message that the Prime Minister sent to them. Canadians have said that we must work together to find ways. This Government has pledged to listen, discuss and plan with
March 25, 1985

Canadians. It has also said that it will act. It has acted and it will continue to act. The next major milestone in this process wil be the Budget in May.
If Hon. Members in the Opposition Parties want to join in this process in a constructive way, we welcome that. However, if they do not choose to listen, pay attention or participate, then so be it, but Canadians have joined with us in this process. Canadians are leaving Members opposite behind. I am sure their constituents will encourage them to get aboard, but if they do not, then the rest of us-all Canadians-will work to solve the economic problems with which we all are faced.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides, for questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said in his speech, in referring to job creation, that 84,000 new jobs since September was not a bad start. How can he say that, when he knows perfectly well that during the six months preceding the advent of this Government, 175,000 jobs had been created? How can he say it is a good thing, when in fact it is a step backwards?
1 have another question about the Minister's speech, which concerns his referring to additional confidence. If this confidence really exists, why does his department expect only a 1.9 per cent increase in employment in 1985?
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry, I did not catch the last question.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister said in his speech that the new Government has created 84,000 jobs since September. He also said that it was just a start. How can he say that when the statistics from Statistics Canada show that before the Conservatives came into power-
No, the second part of the question.

The second part of the question dealt with the fact that the Minister said business has renewed confidence in the economic future. If that is true, why is his own Department projecting an increase of only 1.9 per cent in employment for 1985?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out very simply that the 84,000 figure is better than the performance for the same period 12 months ago. That is why I believe the Hon. Member should be congratulating this Government on its performance in job creation over the past six months.
The second part of his question dealt with renewed confidence. I would tell him that there has been renewed confidence. In my November statement I indicated that real growth
Supply
would probably be about 2.4 per cent. However, increased confidence has been demonstrated by business and consumers. People are demonstrating that confidence by borrowing money to purchase goods from stores. Retail sales have increased by 12 per cent. Canadians are saying that there is better hope, and for that reason real growth has been increased from 2.4 per cent to 2.75 per cent. Other economists have said that they are expecting real growth in excess of 3 per cent for the current year. That is in response to the improved level of confidence which both business and consumers have demonstrated since September 4. It has been during that period of time that confidence has been improving and economists have been increasing their expectations of real growth.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether or not it is a question of language, but I am not sure the Minister answered my question. If the business sector and consumers are so confident with the new Government, why has the Department of Finance, in the paper which was tabled on Saturday morning, projected an increase of only 1.9 per cent in employment for 1985, after the increase of 2.5 per cent in 1984? If the confidence is there, why does the Minister's own Department expect that the increase will be only 1.9 per cent? That will mean the creation of approximately 200,000 jobs, which can be compared to the 255,000 or 260,000 jobs which were created during 1984.
The Minister said that consultation is a good thing. I agree. However, if the consultation during the weekend was serious, why did the Minister say on Friday morning:
we ... will continue the thrust of deficit control in the upcoming budget. To do it, I need your help. The key questions that I hope you will address at this conference are how, how much and how fast.
The Minister clearly stated that cutting the deficit was his main objective and not necessarily job creation. The Minister asked: "How, how much and how fast?" The consultation during the weekend was supposed to have been on those things, but the Minister must have already made up his mind, otherwise he would not have said that.
The Minister compared the consultation during the weekend with that which was held in Australia. The Minister will recall that I asked him last Thursday if the Government was going to table a position paper. That is what happened in Australia. Mr. Speaker, over seven months ago, on September 4, the Canadian people gave to this Government one of the largest majorities in Canadian history. That majority was based on an understanding that the Conservative Government would create employment. To use the words of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in his
Supply
election campaign, "tens of thousands of jobs" would be created as soon as the Conservative Government took office.
Canada had emerged from a severe world recession with an economy that was showing some signs of strength in that inflation and interest rates were down and jobs were being created, although not at a level fast enough to accommodate our very rapidly growing labour force. Canada's record of job creation has been unusually good for many years but we have also had a faster growing labour force than most OECD countries. By the beginning of 1984 some three million more people were employed than had been employed in 1968, but we still had Canadians who wanted work and could not get it. Even the Department of Finance paper which was made available at the weekend conference says that the severe recession in 1981 to 1982 led to a sharp decline in employment, but by the end of 1984 "the level of employment had rebounded above its pre-recession peak. The resulting decline in the unemployment rate was relatively moderate, however, due to large gains in the labour force".
Nevertheless, the Conservative Government came in with assurances that it had the answers to deal with this situation. Here we are, seven and a half months later, with very little new legislation, no Budget, and we now learn there will be no Budget until the end of May. But at least as distressing as the absence of a Budget is the absence of any thoughtful discussion on the state of our economy. There is room for serious discussion. There is room for honest differences of opinion on the best way to proceed at this time in order to ensure that the recovery is durable and that government policies facilitate economic growth and a return to prosperity with full employment.
It is regrettable that the Government has not been willing to have a very full debate on economic policies in the House so that ideas could be examined carefully and thoughtfully. We had an economic statement in the middle of the Throne Speech debate which certainly put severe limits on the possibilities for discussion, and increasingly questions asked in the House on economic matters are being turned back with partisan shots or are the subject of jokes and one-liners. The Government has made no attempt to take Parliament into its confidence, to explain, persuade, advance and develop argument in favour of whatever plans it has for the future. After seven months we are left to guess and draw conclusions from ministerial statements and positions which are often contradictory.
The economic statement on November 8 cut many Government programs, including the National Research Council. Yet the Government is talking about wanting to encourage research and development and innovation. The economic statement emphasized restraint, yet when the Government's Estimates were introduced for the year 1985-86, they were the highest in History and included large additions to the Prime Minister's personal staff and the personal staff of Ministers. The Government talks about creating confidence. Surely a necessary condition for confidence is order and predictability. Yet decisions are made very rapidly or are not made at all. For

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INFUSION OF ADDITIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to advise the House that an agreement was reached this morning to provide the Canadian Commercial Bank with an infusion of capital which will ensure the long-term viability of this Edmonton-based bank. The agreement is a co-operative effort which brings together three Governments, six banks, and the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to provide a support package which will enable this bank to remain viable, thereby protecting the interests of small and medium-sized business in western Canada.
The bank recently experienced a sharp deterioration in its U.S. loan portfolio, particularly as a result of lower oil prices. This situation significantly depressed the value of the Canadian Commercial Bank's loan portfolio. The management of the bank realized that they could not continue to operate a viable banking operation given the magnitude of the problem loans. While many of these loans had been considered manageable, it became evident in recent weeks, given the severity of the situation in the U.S., that a high proportion of them should be written off or significantly reduced on the books of the bank.
March 25, 1985

The management of the bank advised the office of the Inspector General of Banks of the seriousness of the situation on March 14, 1985. Following an analysis by the Inspector General, including on-site re-evaluation of the loan portfolio, it was determined that an important infusion of additional funds was needed to support the continued operation of the bank. It was established that a support package totalling $255 million would be required.
The Government of Alberta was approached by the bank and expressed, at an early stage, its willingness to participate in a support group. The federal Government indicated its willingness to examine ways of providing the necessary assistance. As a result of the negotiations an agreement was reached among members of the support group to provide the $255 million infusion of capital required.
The support package is structured in the following way, Mr. Speaker. The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will provide $75 million. The remaining $180 million will be shared equally by the Province of Alberta, the chartered bank group, and the Government of Canada. The package includes a repayment program which requires the Canadian Commercial Bank to pay 50 per cent of its future pre-tax profits to the participating institutions until the capital is repaid in full. The remaining 50 per cent of the profits will be retained by the bank. No common or preferred share dividends will be paid until the repayment program is complete.
The package also calls for warrants to be issued which, if exercised, would result in substantial dilution of equity held by existing shareholders. In addition, payment of principal and interest on the bank's subordinated debt will be postponed until such time as the members of the support group have been repaid in full.
In a separate arrangement the Governments of Alberta, British Columbia and Canada will be purchasing up to $39 million of the subordinated debt of the bank. The three Governments will share equally in this package. It is a vote of confidence by the members of the support group in the longterm viability of this western-based bank and the economic potential of western Canada, Mr. Speaker.
I know that the House shares our confidence in this regard and stands ready to demonstrate its approval of this positive action. I have been assured by Governor Gerald Bouey that, as usual, the Bank of Canada stands ready to provide liquidity for the Canadian Commercial Bank, if requested, as well as for any other Canadian bank.
