Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying that under the circumstances we can understand why the Government is taking prompt action on this matter. However, having said that, I do not have a number of questions that have to be answered at some point which concern us about this particular action.
First, there is evidence that the bank has been in trouble for some time. What has occurred in the last 48 hours or so, or began officially some two weeks ago on March 14, is what might be described as a request for pressing action that is now being met in an affirmative way by the Government. However, I repeat that there is evidence that the bank had been in some difficulty for some time leading up to March 14. Therefore, why was action not taken prior to today to deal with that situation?
For example, where was the monitoring that ought to have taken place by the Inspector General of Banks on a regular basis? If that monitoring had taken place as a matter of course, it might have led to changes in decisions that would have avoided the current situation which now has to be dealt with by Parliament, the Government of the Province of Alberta and the chartered banks. Why were the warning signals which were out there not adhered to? I am thinking particularly of the collapse of the real estate market in Alberta and of the difficulties in the energy sector, both in Canada and the United States. The bank had a lot of investments in this sector. Serious questions must be asked and answered about the failure to recognize the serious downturn in real estate in the Province of Alberta and the real difficulties in energy.
Third, Mr. Speaker, more than 20 years ago we had the Porter Royal Commission on banks which called for changes in the monitoring procedures that affect our banks and trust companies in particular. The changes that were recommended more than 20 years ago have not been acted upon. If corrective action had been taken in the past two decades, the kind of situation with which the country is now faced-and I am choosing my words with care-might have been avoided.
We have some concerns about the details of this particular bail-out. I appreciate the frankness and helpfulness of both the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) leading up to these statements. They were quite candid in terms of what the Government is involved in here. My understanding of what the Government is involved in is that the people of Canada, via the Government of Canada, are providing an interest-free loan to the bank. If it is not a interest-free loan, we would like to know what the terms are. Through the federal Government the taxpayers of Canada are putting up $60 million and through the Government of Alberta the taxpayers of Alberta are putting up another $60 million. The only guarantee that we will get that money back at all is if this bank turns out to be profitable in the future. We are now in a high-risk situation in terms of returns to the taxpayers for their money.

During periods when the economy is going through a period of adjustments- there can be a serious erosion of the financial positions of governments, corporations, and individuals which may result in the reduced credit worthiness of certain classes of borrowers. Mr. Speaker, I will try to answer both series of questions. In terms of difficulties showing up prior to March 14, the Inspector General monitors all financial institutions on a regular basis and there was no indication before March 14 that there were serious problems within this bank. As Hon. Members, I am sure, are aware, a sudden turn in the financial situation can make the difference between a bank that is dealing appropriately with a difficult situation and something that bears with it the threat of insolvency. This particular problem was triggered by something that happened within the bank's loan portfolio in California which then, of course, created problems within the organization as a whole.
I am aware, if I may say so, of the problems in dealing with financial institutions which the Hon. Member raised around rules which have not been changed for a long time. That is the reason I have indicated before in this House that we intend to produce a paper on financial institutions, how they can better serve this country and how the regulatory supervision can meet
the standards of today in a way that we may not have been able to deal with before.
Let me just deal with the guarantees of repayment. In consultation with the support group, we are satisfied that this bank is now a viable bank, that it will be profitable in the future, and that we will be repaid, as will other members of the support group, out of the future profits of the bank.
There was a question regarding what steps were taken regarding a potential merger. All avenues were explored within the context of the interested parties, and this was the most appropriate way to deal with the problems of the bank. It indicates, I think, the faith of the Province of Alberta, its confidence and our confidence in the ability of the bank in the future, and there is a very significant private sector involvement in this arrangement.
I think the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) raised the same question concerning the role of the Inspector General regarding difficulties. I think I have dealt with that question.
In terms of diversification, the bank had made business decisions to expand into other regions. It expanded into Ontario and into California in an effort to diversify its assets and deposit base. Those were decisions of which the Inspector General was aware. They were appropriate business decisions at the time they were taken. It was in a responsible way, I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the bank was acting in the interests of its depositors by diversifying into other areas.

speechtext:

Canadian Commercial Bank
which suddenly went sour, to whom were they made and in what amounts?

I do not have the list of the particular people and the particular loans, but they were within the energy sector in California which, at the time the loans were made, appeared to have a bright future, but due to the deterioration of oil prices its future was placed in jeopardy.
I should like to return to the question concerning CD1C as a shareholder, and I apologize to the Hon. Member. Through Greymac and Seaway, CDIC is a shareholder in CCB. It has been removed. It is not in that liquidation phase.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INFUSION OF ADDITIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext: I have one final question for the Minister. I am sure that is all you will allow, Mr. Speaker, anyway. For the year 1983, the February 6, 1984 audit result showed a net income decline of 24 per cent from the results of the previous year on a 7 per cent decline in net interest income. For the year 1984, the February 12, 1985 audit result showed a further net income decline of 88 per cent from the previous year on a 10 per cent decrease in net interest income. Given these facts, why did the Inspector General of Banks not come forward to the Government with a report which would have resulted in a closer scrutiny of the activities of the bank during the last 12-month period?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INFUSION OF ADDITIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext: The Inspector General assures me that he has monitored the bank in the appropriate way. A decline in earnings does not necessarily lead to a solvency problem under all circumstances.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INFUSION OF ADDITIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext: A decline in income.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INFUSION OF ADDITIONAL CAPITAL
speechtext: Neither does a decline in income necessarily lead to a solvency problem. It can have that outcome. It does not necessarily have that outcome. In the last year the bank was doing well in two quarters and did not do well in the other two quarters. Therefore, the Inspector General was aware of the progress of the bank. The bank was profitable for the first four or five years of its existence. It was after the national energy policy that it became more difficult and was making very real efforts to act responsibly with regard to its depositors and its borrowers.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INFUSION OF ADDITIONAL CAPITAL

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Minister for making the correction concerning the fact that-

-the fact that Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation was a shareholder in the CCB. separate arrangement the Governments of Alberta, British Columbia and Canada will be purchasing up to $39 million of the subordinated debt of the bank". Is it going to be new subordinated debt or the existing subordinated debt that is going to be bought by those three levels of government?

Mr. Speaker, the self-styled Ronald Reagan of the North, the very Conservative Premier of Ontario, Frank Miller, has finally mustered up enough courage to go to the polls after being reassured by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that his cut-throat budget will only be presented after the next provin-

March 25, 1985

cial election. The Ontario Conservative Party took an active part in the last federal election claiming that it was time for a change, and that having one Party in power for 12 years was too long. That is the same Party that has been in power in Ontario for 42 years.
It will be interesting to watch the Premier make election promises to the people of Ontario. His federal counterpart made 338 promises during his last election campaign and has yet to deliver on almost any of them. The people of Ontario will not be taken twice by the same Conservative Party. They realize that the Government deliberately stalled the presentation of what will be the most treacherous Budget the people of the country will ever see coming from a Government that preaches restraint but turns around and goes on spending for its own benefit.
Eight months of federal Tories is long enough. Forty-three years is way too long.

Mr. Speaker, Indian, Inuit and Metis people have all called for the constitutional recognition and entrenchment of their right to self-government. Before the arrival of early colonists, aboriginal peoples obviously governed themselves, and they have never surrendered the right to do so. In spite of this basic right, federal and provincial Governments imposed laws and regulations on their communities, while industrial and commercial developments eroded their land base and destroyed their traditional economy.
The tragic conditions in most aboriginal communities can only be changed when Canada recognizes the aboriginal peoples' right to self-government and provides resources to make that government effective. However, the working draft from the Federal-Provincial Relations Office only speaks of the right to institutions of self-government where those rights are defined through negotiated agreement. This proposal leaves aboriginal peoples without any bargaining power as they negotiate with provinces. Only if they are lucky enough to reach an agreement can some part of aboriginal self-government be recognized in the Constitution.
The federal Government cannot meet the needs of aboriginal peoples by pursuing the lowest common denominator with the provinces. The right to self-government flows from aboriginal rights. Next week at the constitutional conference the federal Government must give leadership to the provinces and push for full recognition of that right in our Constitution.
I would advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

maintopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION OPPOSITION TO CNCP TELEPHONE SYSTEM APPLICATION
CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION OPPOSITION TO CNCP TELEPHONE SYSTEM APPLICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in Sask-achewan enjoy a good telephone service at reasonable rates. The Province of Saskatchewan built its own telephone system through community participation joining together to create the system as we know it today. It is efficient and economical.
CNCP Telecommunications has made an application to the CRTC for a nation-wide long-distance telephone system that it claims will be cheaper and more efficient. Let us look at the efficiency records of railways.
When I worked on the railway after the Second World War, a parcel could be shipped from Winnipeg, Manitoba, and received in Nipawin, Saskatchewan, within 48 hours. Today it takes so long you may have forgotten what it was you ordered, Mr. Speaker. Telegrams were delivered within hours of the time they were sent. Today, if you have a phone and are available, Mr. Speaker, you may get a telegram the same day, but if not, a telegram takes as long as the mail, and we know what that is like.
Let us not forget previous promises and agreements that were to be in perpetuity but were not kept by the railways. Let us not be lulled into thinking that cheap rates charged by CNCP will continue once our efficient systems are destroyed. The promises of cheap rates will be for the short term. We do not want to have to buy our own telephones and switch boxes as we bought our own boxcars, nor do we want to build new satellites as we did rail lines. The burden on the taxpayer to keep the CNCP conglomerates living high off the hog has reached its limits.

maintopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION OPPOSITION TO CNCP TELEPHONE SYSTEM APPLICATION
speechtext: I would advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, a recent decision by the Federal Court of Appeal to repeal a section of the Customs Tariff that controls the importing of pornographic material into Canada has mobilized the anger of women's groups about the ineffectiveness of this legislation. The present situation is unacceptable, if we realize that for years, women's groups have been making statements, preparing briefs and publicly demonstrating their demands for inclusion in the legislation of a more elaborate and specific definition of the terms "pornography" and "obscenity". Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that in some countries, producers of pornographic material do not hesitate to torture and even

March 25, 1985
kill the actors and actresses who play in these productions, and who are mostly women and children.
Weak legislation that turns a blind eye will only encourage the production of such material. That is why we are asking for amendments to be made to the legislation as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, the women in the riding of Argenteuil-Papineau and women's groups across Canada cannot tolerate a situation where Canadian legislation is encouraging pornography.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the election the unreality of the Conservative promises became apparent. For the first six months the Government busied itself in the politics of style, photo opportunities, and information control. Now the hour of having to make decisions is fast approaching. We have already seen, in the universality debate and in the delays in releasing the unemployment insurance paper, that the shift from the politics of style to the politics of substance will prove to be internally divisive. What will the mighty Prime Minister's Office do to control all the loose cannons on its deck?
The Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) expensive office perceives the media to be a threat. The Prime Minister perceives Parliament to be a threat. The Conservatives learned from the election campaign that the Prime Minister must be isolated to the greatest extent possible, and the Tories have been implementing their own rose garden media strategy.
We remind the Prime Minister that he is not the president of our little state of America yet, and that he is obliged to meet his parliamentary responsibilities, including the attending of Question Period for a change.

subtopic: PROPOSED CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
PROPOSED CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government has proposed drastic and discriminatory changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. On April 1 the Government plans to punish laid-off workers by counting their severance pay for U.I. purposes. I urge the Government to follow the advice given to it by countless labour and business groups and drop this discriminatory provision. If the Government is to follow its own rhetoric in terms of consultation, then it has no option but to abandon this cruel and heartless proposal.

subtopic: GROWTH IN DEMAND FOR GOVERNMENT GRANTS
GROWTH IN DEMAND FOR GOVERNMENT GRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 20 years ago if people in a small town wanted a new arena, they would clump their money together, volunteer their labour, and build it. Today the first thing that happens is the formation of a committee to solicit government funds. This is the legacy of years of Liberal practice when Canadians were bribed with their own money. High taxation meant that people had no excess funds for communal purposes, and the Government enticed people to become dependent on it for handouts.
The attitude exists today that whatever people want to do, whether it be in the field of sports, cultural activities, communal services or, indeed, even private business, they go cap in hand to Government for handouts. The proud spirit of independence that historically characterized Canadians and which has been destroyed by years of Liberal vote buying, must be returned. Grants, giveaways, and handouts must be discontinued so that Canadians can again become, both personally and individually, masters of their own fate.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT'S APPROACH TO REAL NATIONAL CONSENSUS
GOVERNMENT'S APPROACH TO REAL NATIONAL CONSENSUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said nearly two years ago in his book Where I Stand, and I quote:
Our priority must be to restore civilized dialogue and discourse to the partnership of government and to the relationship between the public and private sectors of the country.
Mr. Speaker, after the Throne Speech, after the economic statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), after the First Ministers' Conference in Regina, and after the Quebec Summit, we had the National Economic Conference on employment in Ottawa. This was an occasion without precedent in Canada's history, attracting 136 participants from all walks of life and all regions of this country. There were representatives of the business community, labour, consumers, native peoples, churches, ethnic groups, welfare agencies, the unemployed and the volunteer sector. They all addressed their views to the Prime Minister, and that, Mr. Speaker, is a realistic approach for achieving a truly national consensus.
March 25, 1985

subtopic: DIFFERENCE IN TREATMENT OF ELDERLY SINGLE PEOPLE
DIFFERENCE IN TREATMENT OF ELDERLY SINGLE PEOPLE
speechtext:
Last February 7, Mr. Speaker, I wrote a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to explain the situation of three women in my riding. All three are the same age, 62, all three pay the same monthly rent, $250, and all three get the same monthly welfare allowance, $427.
The only difference between those three women is that the first has been a widow for five years, the second has been separated for five years, and the third is single. I asked on the basis of what social justice the Prime Minister decided that the woman separated for five years and the single woman did not have similar needs and did not deserve assistance under Bill C-26.
Mr. Speaker, if that is the approach of the Prime Minister, I can understand why he did not reply, for he is behaving like a master of ceremonies everywhere in Canada and he has forgotten his responsibilities. I urge all Hon. Members to bring pressure to bear on the Prime Minister to convince him to change Bill C-26 and set $250 million aside for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) rather than waste $610 million on armament.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to call to your attention, and to the attention of Members of this House, the exploits of Steven Fonyo of Vernon, British Columbia.
This committed and dedicated young man, who lost a leg to cancer, has undertaken to run across this great country on his "Journey for Lives", in order to raise funds for cancer research.
Starting in St. John's, Newfoundland, he has steadily worked his way across the country in an awesome effort which has few equals. He has continued to run in the coldest and most difficult weather, even against the advice of his doctors and supporters.
Steven Fonyo has already succeeded in raising a great deal of money. But he has done much more. Through his determination and courage he has provided a great example to millions of Canadians, particularly young Canadians.
We live in difficult times. Young people, and even middle-aged people, are finding it difficult to find employment and to acquire a place in our society. The example of Steve's personal commitment and courage in the face of insurmountable odds has become an inspiration for all of Canada.
Oral Questions
As Steve Fonyo leaves Saskatchewan and runs into Alberta to attain his goal on the Pacific coast, I am certain the Members of this House will wish him Godspeed.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, perhaps one of the reasons the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) finds that consensus on economic problems is so elusive is because the things which the Government continues to allow to happen belie the rhetoric which is in vogue these days about co-operation, consultation, and the new era of labour-management relations.
The House will recall that last week I raised the matter of the layoffs at CN and the fact that hundreds of people were being laid off while the company and the unions were in conciliation on a no layoff contract. At that time I also mentioned that those workers were given a two-week notice. The CNR is hiding behind a regulation in the Canada Labour Code which allows it to waive the normal period of notice if workers are receiving supplementary benefits of any kind. The fact of the matter is that most of the people who are to be laid off have not worked for the company for the required two-year period and, therefore, will receive no supplementary unemployment benefits.
In my view, and in the view of anyone who takes a good look at it, the CNR is being allowed to violate the spirit and the letter of the Canada Labour Code, insofar as there will be workers who will only receive two weeks' notice about their layoff but who will not receive supplementary benefits. Those workers should have had the notice which is required under the Canada Labour Code.
If the Government is serious about its rhetoric it will tell the CNR to smarten up and give those people the notice that they should have received, or, for that matter, it should cancel the layoffs altogether.
Order, please.

Mr. Speaker, after the economic summit which ended on Saturday after-

March 25, 1985
Oral Questions
noon, Mr. Andre Marcoux, representing unemployed youth, said the following, and I am quoting from the Gazette of March 25:

I did not come here expecting miracles, but I expected more than this.

Mr. Speaker, once again, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, in the absence of the Right Hon. Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister, whether the results of this economic conference would not have been more positive for young unemployed Canadians like Mr. Marcoux and many others, if this had followed the example of the Australian Government and submitted specific proposals to conference participants which would then have been used to establish a consensus.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is very clear that there was a good deal of positive response in the various statements which were made by a number of the participants at the conference following its completion on Saturday afternoon. I can tell the House, and particularly the Hon. Member, that a number of the people spoke personally to me and indicated that they were very pleased with the results of the conference.
With respect to the specific question of the Hon. Member, we did have a document which formed the basis of the discussion at the economic conference. It was the economic statement of November 8. That has been the basis of the consultation process in all the areas which were covered. A very large number of areas were covered in the economic statement, and that statement has been the basis for consultation during the period since November 8 last.

subtopic: IMPACT OF BUDGETARY CUTBACKS ON EMPLOYMENT GROWTH
IMPACT OF BUDGETARY CUTBACKS ON EMPLOYMENT GROWTH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the November 8 document was among the papers to be discussed at the conference, why was it not on any of the tables where papers prepared by academics were being distributed? Mr. Speaker, as far as job creation is concerned, during the conference the Minister of Finance tabled statistics indicating that in 1985, employment growth will be only 1.9 per cent, compared with 2.5 per cent in 1984. Has the Minister already allowed for the budget cuts that are to be announced later on in predicting this very low figure for 1985?

subtopic: IMPACT OF BUDGETARY CUTBACKS ON EMPLOYMENT GROWTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we came into office on September 4 last, it was very clear that we were facing a slower economy in 1985. I indicated that in the economic statement which I made on November
8.	I should point out that since then, we, as well as many other economic commentators, have indicated that the projections which they made, and the projections which the Government made in November, should be increased because of the
improved confidence in the economy and, specifically, the improved economic results in retail sales, manufacturing, investment intentions, and the production and sales of manufacturing companies. There is a large number of specific economic indicators which show that things have picked up since September 4, and I would suggest to the Hon. Member that it is related to the economic statement which we presented on November 8.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION ON CREATION OF DIMINISHING NUMBER OF JOBS
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION ON CREATION OF DIMINISHING NUMBER OF JOBS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the situation has improved so much since September 4, could the Minister explain why during the last six months of the Liberal administration, 175,000 jobs were created and why during the first six months his Government has been in power, only 84,000 have been created?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION ON CREATION OF DIMINISHING NUMBER OF JOBS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member asked that question before lunch, and I will give him the same answer. If we compare the 84,000 or 86,000 jobs which have been created since September with the identical period in the previous year, we find that the 86,000 figure is a good deal higher than the figure in the previous year. I think that is a good performance. I do not know why he is walking around under a little black cloud pointing out all the bad things, when there are a lot of very good things about which people are very pleased.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION ON CREATION OF DIMINISHING NUMBER OF JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In late February the European Economic Community filed formal complaints against Canada with GATT, protesting the continuation of import quotas. The EEC notified GATT concerning its retaliatory measures against selected imports, including styrene monomer, which would be effective as of April 1. Polysar, a company based in my riding of Sarnia-Lambton, has a worldscale styrene facility and is the only exporter, with exports valued at $30 million per year.
Would the Minister of Finance respond to these concerns and tell the House if we are proceeding in negotiations to alleviate the possibility of higher duties? And are we trying to obtain complete removal of styrene from the list of products included in the retaliatory act?
March 25, 1985

subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the Hon. Member is very concerned about this matter, as are we in the Government. There are negotiations under way with the European Community authorities on this question.
As the Hon. Member knows, the threats by the European Community are in response to the actions taken by the Government to try to slow down the very happy exports from the European Community of veal and beef. We are in the course of trying to reach some satisfactory resolution of the matter. I am very much aware of the concerns of the Hon. Member, and 1 will keep him posted as these negotiations proceed.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Earlier today the Secretary of State for Finance announced that the Government was involved in a massive bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank. This involves $60 million in direct funding from the people of Canada through the federal Government in the form of an interest free pay-out, and another $60 million to come from the people of Alberta through their Government. The Minister of State said that there was no evidence that the bank in question was in difficulty until March 14 of this year. Would the Minister of Finance confirm that an official from the Inspector General of Banks informed him last September that this bank was in difficulty?

Mr. Speaker, I would confirm to the Leader of the New Democratic Party that, yes, in September I received notification from the Inspector General of Banks to the effect that he was aware of the difficulty which the Canadian Commercial Bank was having with its earnings and was monitoring the situation closely, as is the normal course when banks do experience this type of weakness in their earnings.
There was no suggestion at that time that there was any question of a risk of insolvency. That risk did come to the attention of the Inspector General of Banks on March 14, as my colleague indicated earlier today in the House. We have taken very speedy action in response to the notification by the Canadian Commercial Bank to the Inspector General of Banks, who immediately brought both the Minister of State and myself into the picture.

Mr. Speaker, what the Minister is now saying certainly departs from the implication which was left by the Minister of State at one o'clock today when she said that the Government had no sign before March 14 that the bank was in difficulty. What the Minister of Finance is now saying is that he was warned last September
Oral Questions
that the bank was in some difficulty, or that it was drawn to his attention.
Since the Government is now proposing that the taxpayers, through the federal Government and through the Government of Alberta, put up $120 million in interest-free loans to bail out this bank, why did the Government not use the time since last September to get the chartered banks of Canada-which are the most profitable in the world-to assume their responsibility in the private sector to move in and take corrective action and rationalize this bank without involving a bail-out from the taxpayers of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, let me make it quite clear that what I am saying to the Hon. Member now is not inconsistent in any way with what the Minister of State said before lunch. What she said at that time, and what I said a minute ago, is that when the Inspector General of Banks became aware of this, he increased his surveillance of the bank in the normal way, as he would do in any situation where there is some deterioration in the normal operations of a chartered bank. During this period of time there had been a continued surveillance, but there had been no question of the solvency of the bank until it received the shock of the write-down which it was required to take on some of its operations in California. When that shock did occur, it pointed up the need for further action by the Government of Canada, and we responded very quickly to that need.

Mr. Speaker, I am informed that the kind of follow-up action taken by the Government consisted simply of the officials of the Inspector General of Banks making two or three additional visits to the Canadian Commercial Bank since it was said to be in trouble last September. I would say that this is hardly excessive monitoring of the system. Therefore, since the taxpayers of Canada have a lot of money at stake in this operation, will the Government do two things? Will it immediately establish a special committee of the House to look into the details of the proposed action of the Government? Second, will it mandate this committee to study the regulations pertaining to banks and trust companies over a two-month period only, and come back to the House with very specific recommendations so that we can avoid this situation in the future?

Mr. Speaker, let me point out that this situation, as the Hon. Member refers to it, is a very unusual circumstance. It happens very, very rarely in Canadian banking practice. I believe this is one of the reasons why the Canadian banking system is regarded around the world as one of the strongest banking systems in any country involved in the international community.
Hear, hear!

Let me remind the Hon. Member of what my colleague said before lunch. She is in the

March 25, 1985
Oral Questions
course of preparing, and will be releasing shortly, a paper on financial institutions which will cover the very important question of bank regulations and the whole monitoring process. I would think that at that time there will be many opportunities for Hon. Members to become more involved in making recommendations and commenting on current practices of the Inspector General of Banks and the Government of Canada in monitoring our chartered banks.
More discussions.

subsubtopic: PETITION AGAINST CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. At the weekend conference perhaps the one clear agreement which appeared was when 87 of the 136 participants signed a petition requesting that the changes in the unemployment insurance which are due to come into force next week, and which have the effect of making people who receive severance pay or pension benefits when laid off lose several weeks on unemployment insurance benefits, not go ahead. Would the Minister say whether she is prepared to respond to that request?

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: PETITION AGAINST CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House knows, these measures were announced in the economic statement of last November. I had the opportunity then of discussions over a number of weeks with representatives of business and labour in order to determine the fairest way in which these changes could be implemented. As a result of that, we announced a phased-in method which would come into effect at the end of this month. We think that is the fairest way to go about it, and those changes will be implemented accordingly.
I would say to the Hon. Member that what was apparent at that conference was that the unemployment insurance program is not meeting the challenges of our changing society. Therefore, the consensus which was expressed by everyone-

subsubtopic: PETITION AGAINST CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
speechtext: With great respect, the Minister's answer is verging on a speech.
Mr. Speaker, following on the question the Minister raised about a broader look at unemployment insurance, may I know if we are going to have a discussion paper on that?

Mr. Speaker, that has yet to be determined. However, as I was saying, one of the consequences of the discussion in the workshop on unemployment insurance was a
very real consensus that the Act needs to be reviewed. One aspect I would think would be included is the question of labour economic adjustment and how the unemployment insurance program can be better tailored to those needs.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF HON. FRANQOIS NGARUKIYINTWALI, MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS AND CO-OPERATION. OF RWANDA
PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF HON. FRANQOIS NGARUKIYINTWALI, MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS AND CO-OPERATION. OF RWANDA
speechtext: Order, please. I would like to draw the attention of the House to the presence in our gallery of Mr. Francois Ngarukiyintwali, Minister of External Affairs and Co-operation of Rwanda.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Earlier today the Minister of State for Finance, in presenting a statement to the House about the Canadian Commercial Bank bail-out operation, said that the federal Government will be providing some $73 million, consisting of $60 million as an interest-free infusion of funds and $13 million as its share of a purchase of subordinated debt. Will these millions of dollars from the federal Government come from an addition to the deficit or from the cutting of programs? If the latter, which programs are going to be cut?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member will understand that this particular support operation for the CCB was put together on very short notice. I can tell him that the final agreement was not reached until shortly before seven o'clock this morning, so we have not had any opportunity to consider the questions that the Hon. Member has put forward.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say that is rather surprising. When one has to deal with amounts in the tens of millions of dollars, in this case $73 million, I would think one would give some consideration to where they are going to come from. That is not a very good example of sound financial management.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today the Minister of State for Finance said that some $90 million in loans are going to be written off by the Canadian Commercial Bank. If this is the case I would like the Minister of Finance to explain why there is a rescue operation totalling
March 25, 1985

some $394 million, of which some $73 million comes from the federal Government alone?

I am not sure 1 understand the import of the question. Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking earlier, I had begun to talk about trade arrangements between Canada and the United States. I had been pointing out that while our relationship with out greatest ally and chief trading partner is extremely important to us, it is also important that we negotiate well in all these matters because the United States has certainly shown itself very adroit in protecting its own interests in the past.
The United States complained long and hard about our Foreign Investment Review Agency, but that country itself prohibits or restricts foreign investment in many sectors of its economy-in coastal and freshwater shipping, aviation, nuclear and hydro generating, communications, financial industries, real estate, fishing, some mineral leases, dredging and salvaging operations, and the defence industries. As the House knows, the net of defence industries is cast very wide.
A comparison of relative investment is quite interesting. For instance, mining is approximately 40 per cent foreign controlled in Canada and approximately 5 per cent in the United States; oil and gas, something between 50 per cent and 60 per cent foreign controlled in Canada as against 18 per cent in the U.S.; and manufacturing, something around 48 per cent foreign controlled in Canada compared with 3 per cent in the United States. The whole basis on which to consider investment policy in the two countries is different.
The U.S. economy, which is so greatly admired by the Government opposite, is not without problems. Some of those problems may impact upon us unless we plan carefully to protect ourselves. The United States has an enormous trade deficit. If at some point it becomes concerned about it and decides to act on it, we will certainly be open to injury. For instance, Ontario alone exports more into the United States than does Japan. The United States also has an enormous deficit which, of course, is fuelled by enormous defence spending. This is a situation which may change. International banking institutions may very well become concerned about the fact that the United States is so greatly over-extended by some standards. If there are major changes in the way the international community looks at this, we might be very vulnerable if indeed we have put all our eggs into that basket without proper negotiation and safeguards.
Approximately 80 per cent of our trade is now with the United States. Does the Government plan to leave that more or less as it is and to continue, as did the Liberal Government, to encourage exporters to find other markets, particularly Pacific Rim countries, or is the intention to lock us in more closely with the United States? These are things to which we should know the answers.
In talking about trade arrangements, particularly a trade treaty with the United States, it is impossible to do that unless one also looks at the whole question of emerging technologies, emerging competition from the less developed countries, the effect of this on our own industries and the need to protect our people, be it with retraining grants or labour adjustment programs. This whole package needs to be considered very carefully.
It may very well be that the Government is considering all this, but we do not know because less and less is being debated in this House. More and more is being dealt with by way of press release and statements outside the House. There are very few things that are more important to us than the present state of the economy. All of us were elected by people who have had
March 25, 1985

an enormously difficult time living through the recession. They are hurting and are looking for some help.
When we began this session, the position of the Official Opposition was, and still is, that any measures that are put forward by the Government that are constructive we will support. That is still our position, but it gets increasingly difficult because we are not seeing measures introduced in the House. Our questions are not answered. They are responded to by one-liners. The Government seems to be still fighting the last election.
May I end by making a plea that this Government proceed to take its responsibilities, give leadership and take us into its confidence. Try and deal in a civilized and responsible fashion with the Members of the Opposition, and you will find very ready co-operation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the motion before the House today introduced by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) on behalf of the Liberal Party. The motion condemns the Government for not bringing in a Budget by this time. It talks about the importance of jobs in this country and mentions many groups in our society, such as young people, farmers, fishermen, the elderly and native people.
I want to say at the outset that I cannot recall in all my years in the House a newly elected Goverment taking so long to bring in a Budget. Last November, of course, we had an economic statement by the Government. In that statement we saw some indication of the way this Government wants to go. We saw them being Liberals once again. They brought in the 1 per cent increase in the sales tax which the Liberal Minister of Finance, "old ironclad", introduced in this House about a year or so ago. They announced that they would increase the price of fuel in this country up to the world level. That showed some indication of where this Government wants to go.
We saw in the economic statement the program of restraint being practised by the Government whereby it cut several billion dollars off government spending. I assume by doing this, instead of creating jobs in this country the Government is creating more unemployment. It was slowing down the national economy, putting less money into the hands of ordinary Canadians. Therefore, ordinary Canadians had less money to spend.
That is the opposite direction that we as a nation should be going at this time. I remember very well the election campaign of last summer. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), then Leader of the Opposition, said time and time again across this country that there were really three issues in the campaign: jobs, jobs, jobs. At that time I expected that if the Conservatives won the election, we would have an early Budget and the emphasis would be on job creation. I was very surprised to see that Budget put off by several months and to see it further delayed now until the latter part of the month of May. He has
Supply
broken a campaign promise. He has a very important mandate to deliver jobs for ordinary Canadians.
On September 4 there were about 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. As I stand here today at the end of March, there are still about 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. Where is the difference? What changes have there been in terms of what the Prime Minister has done?
I remember the beginning of July when the Prime Minister held a caucus with some of his western candidates in the City of Prince Albert. He said: "Elect me as Prime Minister and overnight there will be the creation of thousands of jobs". I know wise Members like the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) would not have made that kind of statement. He knows there is nothing magical about this. It is no wonder the Government failed. It could not create those jobs overnight.
Let us look at the most recent unemployment stats that came out a few weeks ago for the month of February. I find that unemployment in Canada in the last year has gone up in seven of our ten provinces. We find that in almost all parts of Canada. The unemployment rate is getting worse instead of better. That is why the priority of this House has to be the creation of jobs. That has to be the priority.
I was very disappointed at the reaction of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) at the National Economic Conference held in Ottawa a few days ago. There seemed to be a big split. The bankers and big business on one side were saying that the priority of this country had to be the deficit; to cut back on the deficit was the way to go, in the direction of Billy Bennett of British Columbia. That seemed to be what the bankers and big business were saying.
On the other side we had community groups, labour and other groups representing ordinary Canadians which said that the most important priority has to be the creation of jobs. One of the consequences of the creation of jobs in this country is that in the long run it would bring down the deficit in Canada. We would once again become a nation of producers, a nation of doers, producing goods and commodities for Canadians, producing those things that we can use in this country. If we bring down the unemployment rate, we would also be reducing the pay-out from the federal Government of unemployment insurance funds and reducing the pay-out from provincial Governments of welfare cheques.
For the life of me, I do not know why the Government goes through a consultation process if it is not going to listen to what it hears and if it is not going to act on what Canadians are saying. It is very clear that they are saying that the deficit is not the priority. They are saying the Government should spend money to create jobs, help small business, the farmers, fishermen and loggers. They say it should help the base industries in this country and from there there will be a ripple-up effect and the creation of jobs in this country. Instead of that ripple-up, this Minister is following some of the old Liberal policies of a trickle-down theory: government welfare for the rich, government welfare for the banks and the big companies, government welfare for those that have while the ordinary citizen has to pay a bigger and bigger tax bill.

March 25, 1985
Supply
1 am sure some of the Tory back-benchers are embarrassed by their Government's continuation of old Liberal policies. I ask those back-benchers to rise and say what they think and to make sure that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) keeps his promise that the most important priority in the country is jobs. As it was during the campaign, the most important priority in Parliament must be jobs. That is the reason we were all elected. That is our mandate. Yet we see no significant improvement whatsoever in job creation in the country.
During the last two months, I along with the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) and other members of this caucus had an opportunity to go across the country to speak to ordinary Canadians about jobs and about the future of our land. Two or three things I heard struck me as being very significant. First, the people say unanimously that the priority of this Parliament must be jobs and that politicians should stop fighting and bickering and come up with some national vision indicating how we might create those jobs.
Second, and I was surprised when I heard this in places like Newfoundland, the Canadian people are hopeful that something can be done. They are optimistic. There is hope in the face of adversity. There is hope that we as a country can get our act together and create jobs for Canadians from coast to coast.
The third thing that struck me was that there is a national consensus among Canadians from one part of Canada to the other that there are no magical solutions and no experts in national economic policy. Instead, they feel we should be putting a lot more say and a lot more money into the hands of ordinary Canadians from coast to coast so that ordinary Canadians in each community may control the economy of their own particular community.
Canadians are saying that we need more programs directed toward self-reliance in the various communities across the country. They say we need more programs to promote small business and worker co-ops and that there should be more programs to promote local municipalities so that they can have a say over the direction their community is headed.
I found that if there was a major theme in terms of critiques of what has happened in the past and up until now, it has been that we have had too many programs that have been centrally imposed on communities from coast to coast, that we have had insensitive bureaucracy and insensitive, centralized government that does not understand the needs of ordinary folk from one part of Canada to the other. I will never forget that in Newfoundland we heard criticism of over-centralization not just in Ottawa but also in St. John's. We heard that the provincial capitals are not giving enough assistance to the people to enable them to make their own local decisions. I am speaking of more economic and industrial democracy so that farmers will have more say over farm policies and fishermen will have more say over fisheries policies. There should be more assistance to small businesses and local co-op groups in order to allow them to do things on their own.
The projects to which I have referred may not be large projects. There has been a great deal of criticism of megaprojects, those grandiose schemes that over a few years would create tens and tens of thousands of jobs. Ordinary folk are talking about creating five or six jobs here and 10 or 20 jobs there. In British Columbia the same can be said of the logging industry. We could begin to process and manufacture more of our wood products in our own country. On the Prairies there are all kinds of ideas about building on our bases of grain and oil. We could give more federal Government assistance and aid to local and community initiatives thought up by ordinary people.
Time and time again it was pointed out to me that ordinary people had a much better idea about what would be viable in their own communities than some bureaucrat in Ottawa or some bureaucrats in the provincial capitals. This is the direction ordinary Canadians tell us they wish to take. They want a Government that will respond to that wish. They want more funding for local initiatives and worker co-ops. They want more technical assistance in the setting up and establishing of worker co-ops. The Government should take a look at the experiences of France and Spain with regard to worker co-ops. The people want more aid and assistance to small business.
There was a lot of criticism of government policy. We were told that too much is given to big business. Approximately 70 per cent to 80 per cent of funding to business goes to big businesses like the oil companies and very little goes to small business, the sector in which most of the jobs are created in the first place. That is the direction ordinary Canadians wish to take.
In addition, we heard that we should have a made-in-Canada interest rate policy. If we were to have a made-in-Canada interest rate policy and we brought down the real interest rate by 3 or 4 per cent, we would kick-start the economy. We could provide low-interest loans to home owners, farmers, fishermen and small business people so they could expand their businesses, build houses and put up structures across the nation. This would put Canadians back to work. Many countries have done that. However, it seems to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is afraid to take a step that is out of sync with the steps taken by Mr. Reagan in the United States.
It seems to me, and I am sure the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) would agree with me, that there is a two-pronged economic policy in Canada. The Government relies on private sector big businesses and on the United States and Mr. Reagan. Those are the two things upon which the Government relies for economic recovery in Canada. We say that that will not work. That will not put Canadians back to work. We must start doing things on our own. Interest rate policy is very important and I think that is something to which the Government must address itself.
The Conservative Premier of Alberta spoke about a real interest rate in Canada of approximately 4 per cent. With the rate of inflation at 3.5 per cent or 4 per cent, he is talking
March 25, 1985

about a 7 per cent interest rate rather than the 11 per cent interest rate we now have which is set by the Bank of Canada.
I ask a very sincere question, Mr. Speaker. Sitting in the chair, I know you must ask this question of yourself very often, Mr. Speaker. What is the difference between the previous Liberal Government and the Government that sits across the way?
[ Translation]
We still have the same Public Service, the same President of the Bank of Canada and the same Deputy Minister to the Minister of Finance in this country. We have the same monetary policy. There is someone down there who agrees with me. He said he agreed. He happens to be a Conservative backbencher.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that the present Government's monetary policy is exactly what we had under the Trudeau Government two or three years ago. Mr. Bouey is taking the Government's decisions, not the Minister of Finance, and I am sure the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) will agree, because 1 remember distinctly that when he was on this side of the House two or three years ago, he often asked why we did not have an independent monetary policy in this country. He often spoke about about the need for helping small- and medium-sized businesses, farmers and fishermen and for helping average Canadians with their mortgages. I ask you, Mr. Speaker: What is the difference?
There is no difference!

There is no difference. Mr. Mulroney is a reincarnation of Mr. Trudeau. Everything is exactly the same. There may be a slight difference ... I think Mr. Mulroney is fonder of Mr. Reagan than Mr. Trudeau, but I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that is the only difference.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly on the details of the motion. The motion was introduced by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) and reads as follows:
That this House regrets that the Government has further postponed a budget thereby assuring that it will have gone more than eight months in office without taking any concrete action to create jobs and to establish the kind of economic confidence necessary for the realization of the hopes and aspirations of all
Supply
Canadians, in particular, women, young people, farmers, fishermen, the elderly, natives and, above all, the almost one-and-one half million unemployed.
I would like to move an amendment as follows: I move seconded by the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young):
That the motion be amended by inserting immediately after the word "natives" the following words:
"the disabled population, visible minorities".
1 do that because the Liberals have listed a whole series of people, including native people, farmers and fishermen, but two very important groups in our society have been forgotten-the disabled and the visible minorities.
The Abella report was tabled in the House in November. That report talked about affirmative action and employment equity for four groups in Canada. It studied women and three minorities-natives, disabled people and visible minorities. I think it was an oversight on behalf of the Liberal Party to single out a couple of the groups which were studied and forget about the disabled and the visible minorities.
In our action group on jobs, we found that Canadians tend to forget about the disabled. However, between 8 per cent and 10 per cent of Canadians are disabled. In terms of jobs, most of those people are discriminated against. Over the years, the federal Government has been very lax in providing adequate assistance in the Canada Employment Centres in terms of finding jobs for disabled citizens and in terms of training programs for disabled Canadians. Three or four years ago, Parliament established the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. Our spokesman on the committee was the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young). He has made speech after speech in the House about the necessity for positive programs for disabled Canadians. The national organizations which represent disabled Canadians are disappointed that the Government has not taken enough positive action on their behalf. Therefore, if we are to discuss this motion today, we must as well do something for disabled Canadians.
Of course, the other group is that of the visible minorities. We all know that visible minorities have problems in terms of discrimination on the job and in job searches. In Toronto, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) and I spoke with a representative of the National Black Coalition, as well as people from other organizations which deal with racism. We were told about different studies which had been carried out in Toronto, and that it was evident from those studies that black people and visible minorities were discriminated against by employers. In one particular study, a black actor and a white actor went to various employers in the City of Toronto to apply for the same job. They had the same qualifications, the same general education and they were the same age. They also used the same approach. They found that time and time again the jobs would disappear when the black actor applied, but often an offer would be made to the white actor who applied either a few minutes before or a few minutes after the black actor.
It is time that we started to think more about and do more for visible minorities. In the City of Halifax we met with church groups which spoke about the problems of the black
Supply
population. It is wrong for the vast majority of black young people in the City of Halifax to be unemployed. It is wrong and it is unfair in a city and a country which has so much to offer. We must take a strong stand in this House on behalf of visible minorities and handicapped people, as well as those who are mentioned in the Liberal motion.
I appeal to the House to support our amendment. Also, in closing, I appeal to the House to fulfil the mandate which we have as parliamentarians-that the first priority is to create jobs. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) should stop listening to the bankers and big business in Canada and start listening to ordinary Canadians, small business, farmers, workers and fishermen from one end of Canada to the other. They will tell him a different story.
In the election campaign last summer, the politician who spoke the most about the deficit was the Leader of the Liberal Party. We saw what happened to him on September 4. I believe that Canadians delivered a message on that particular issue. The Government should not forget that message as it sets national economic priorities and prepares the Budget which will be brought down in the next couple of months.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that anyone who has been associated with it will agree that employment is the key issue to the disabled community in Canada. Without access to adequate and decent employment, the disabled population is denied access to every other opportunity which every able-bodied Canadian expects to have as a matter of right. Without adequate employment opportunities, people are denied access to decent housing, transportation and education. Many Members are not aware that there are thousands of kids in Canada who are disabled-either developmental^ handicapped or otherwise-and who are completely denied access to education across Canada. If we hope to provide disabled Canadians with equal access to transportation, education, recreation and communication, the key element is the access to employment opportunities.
Could the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) tell us if any witnesses came before the task force on jobs, to which he referred, to give evidence on the lack of employment opportunities adequate training and government assistance, which, if adequate, would provide those employment opportunities?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, we heard from organizations which represented disabled Canadians. Their main concern was jobs and how they felt discriminated against. Indeed, ,hey felt that municipal, provincial and federal parliamentarians had forgotten about them in the planning and organization of our society. I remember speaking with a gentleman who I believe was the president of an organization for disabled people in Halifax. He told us that the federal Government, in the Department of Employment and Immigration, had only
March 25, 1985
one co-ordinator to deal with disabled people in the Atlantic provinces. He also said-and I have not had a chance to check this-that the Department had one co-ordinator in Quebec, one in Ontario and one or two in the West. He pointed out that too little priority had been given to the needs and aspirations of disabled Canadians. He put forward several recommendations as to what should be done to improve the situation. The other point which he mentioned was that the recommendations which were made by Judge Abella concerning disabled Canadians should be implemented. His concern was that all the good sentiments in the world and all the voluntary guidelines probably would not work. He said that if these affirmative action and employment equity programs were going to work there would have to be mandatory regulations and guidelines with specific targets, goals and objectives. However, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has not provided that. We heard the fear expressed that without those specific targets and goals-as has been proven elsewhere-it would not work in Canada.
Once again, I would refer to the task force which was agreed to by all Parties in the House during the last Parliament. In the report of that task force many other recommendations were made for which disabled people in Canada are pushing very hard.

Mr. Speaker, I submit that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), in the course of his speech-as other New Democratic Members have done for some months and, indeed, years-has embarked on a sematical word which I believe is dangerous and misleading. They say that they are the defenders of the ordinary Canadian. Obviously, that view has a great deal of attractiveness in the hearts of Canadians. It naturally would, because all Canadians believe they are ordinary. I believe Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party should be called to task for using the word "ordinary" repeatedly as they do. Do they have an operative definition of who is ordinary? Why is it that those Hon. Members, as a Party, cannot support people who are imaginative, unique or extraordinary? Why do they create a caste system which sets certain groups of people aside and then say, "We will defend those people"? Would the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) stand in his place and give us an operative definition of an ordinary Canadian? Who belongs to that limited group which those Hon. Members, if they were ever in Government, would pretend to support? Who are that narrow bunch of Canadians?
You are, Arnold.

Mr. Speaker, I think a good example is the question I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) today about assistance to one of the banks and the fact that the taxpayers are giving an interest-free loan of several millions of dollars to this particular bank. I do not consider banks to be representatives of ordinary Canadians. I asked the Minister whether or not this bill will be a precedent for interest-free loans. In other words, would farmers receive the same kind of

March 25, 1985

consideration? A lot of farmers are going bankrupt across this country.
Who do you think borrows from the banks?
When was the last time you got an interest-free loan from the bank?

The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) asks me who I think borrows from the banks. I have a lot of farmers in my riding who borrow from the banks and those banks are charging these farmers usurious interest rates right now.
Right on.

I know the Minister does not agree with that, but her seat-mate does. I know he agrees because he knows a fair amount about the ordinary citizens in his own riding. I can point out all kinds of farmers in my riding who are in difficulty and I am asked time and time again: if there are going to be interest-free loans for the banks or bail-outs of big companies, why can't we give the same consideration to ordinary farmers, fishermen or small business people? What is good for the goose should be good for the gander, I say to the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone). Why that difference? Is that what "Progressive Conservative" means? I know it is a continuation of the policies of the old Liberal Government. I do not like it. I do not find Canadians like it either. But that is what we mean by "ordinary Canadians".

Mr. Speaker, I would certainly want to draw to the attention of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville that when we protect a bank from going bankrupt, we not only protect the bank but we protect all of the investors and the people who use that bank. The Hon. Member knows that if we should let the banks go into default, there would be literally thousands of Canadians-who the Hon. Member has just bracketed as "ordinary" Canadians-who would end up being very badly crushed. When the Hon. Member gives his thesis that he is for small business, he really is saying he is for small business until the small business becomes successful. As soon as it becomes successful, he is no longer with it. Those Hon. Members only want to be for the little fellow.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would like the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville to know that the creation of jobs throughout the country is dependent upon the imaginations and ingenuity of Canadians everywhere. Certainly, to present some kind of euphoric notion that there is a group of people across Canada who are unordinary, who do not belong to this caste system the New Democratic Party supports, is not at all in keeping with the nature of this country. Any Government which comes to power ought to be a Government which stands for all Canadians, for all productivity. It should not try to create a caste system, as the NDP are doing, by picking out a group of people here and there and saying, "Those are the ones we support, the rest be darned". That Party seems to take the view that it is for the little businessman. What happens to the
Supply
little businessman when he becomes successful? The NDP casts him aside. He is no longer ordinary.
The Hon. Member did not give an operative definition of an "ordinary" Canadian, he cannot think of one.
You weren't listening.
He may not have time to respond now but he can write me a letter. I challenge him to give me a definition of an "ordinary" Canadian, because every Canadian is an ordinary Canadian.
Give him a chance.
Sit down and give him a chance.

Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party who shout "sit down", thus showing disrespect for this Parliament, should know very well that they cannot continue to get away with appealing with semantic words which tug at the heart-strings of Canadians without ever being called to account. The words they use over and over again in fact are meaningless. Those Hon. Members have no operative definition. They should start dealing only in facts and not in pure rhetoric.

Mr. Speaker, as I listen to the Hon. Member for Crowfoot, I think he must have listened carefully over the years to Ernest Manning. The Hon. member certainly follows Ernest Manning's tradition in the way he speaks in this House.
If the Hon. Member wants a precedent, Mr. Speaker, where a Government did not bail out a bank, I can tell him that the Conservative Government of Saskatchewan did not bail out Pioneer Life. That is a precedent. I suppose this Government would like to bail them out. I am not exactly sure where it stands. What I am saying is that if the Hon. Member for Crowfoot wants to find some ordinary Canadians, he should come to my riding and I will introduce him to the farmers in my riding who are very ordinary Canadians and who would like the same kinds of breaks from the federal Government as it is giving to the banks. If the Hon. Member wants to continue standing up for rich Canadians, that is fine with me, but there will be an election in this country in three or four years and the population will respond. If the Conservatives are as insensitive as the Liberals were a few years ago, they will go the same way as the Liberal Party.

Mr. Speaker, it is always refreshing to hear the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) with respect to bail-outs. It was only last week that the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) was complaining to the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) that she would not come to the assistance of the Pioneer Trust Company. This morning, the Hon. Member's own confrere from Hamilton was making the same complaint. Now we hear the Hon. Member complaining about the fact that the Minister of State for Finance was able to organize

largely a private sector agreement to come to the assistance of the Canadian Commercial Bank so that all sorts of small depositors, small business people in the Edmonton area, would not lose their shirts completely.
The Hon. Member knows, and ought to know, that the economy of western Canada is, to a large extent, in tatters, mainly because of the national energy policy. He knows that if that bank had gone bankrupt-and it would have had there not been assistance from Canadian banks, from the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, from the Province of Alberta, and from the federal Government-all sorts of small business people would have lost everything.
