Member for Yorkton-Melville that the people participating in the arrangement will be able to participate further in the profitability of the bank as they take up share warrants in connection with the arrangements.
This motion is perhaps the most ridiculous motion which has ever come before this House. I am indeed surprised that the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) would ever bring a motion of this nature to this House of Commons. The Hon. Member complains that a budget has not come out as if a budget was the only thing a government does. Those Hon. Members have some idea that governments are here to make budgets. Surely governments are here to run the country. And this country is being turned around, and has been turned around from September 4 until now. A budget will be produced in due course. There is a lot which has to be done which does not and did not require budgetary help.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville, for example, said that when he went around the country he found that Canadians were tired of being oppressed by the central Government in Ottawa. He said there was no sense of co-operation and we cannot pass rules in Ottawa which are enforced in towns across the country such as Vancouver and Saint John. That is right. We understand that. That is why we have been able, for the first time in some 15 or 16 years, finally to get the provinces and the federal Government together. This way we can have a consensus on how we should proceed with medicare, education, retraining.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) made a deal with the provincial Ministers of Labour and Employment to get summer work for students in a new job-creation program, a program which is working darn fine in my riding. People are offering jobs to students for the first time because they now feel the Government of Canada understands their requirements. They want to co-operate, get aboard and be part of building Canada. They want to give the youth of Canada an opportunity. We have a Government that understands business, the provinces, labour and all those elements in the economy who want to work together. This motion says that nothing has been done about job creation, but that is just not so.
The motion goes on to refer to the economic confidence necessary for the realization of the hopes and aspirations of Canadians. Let us talk about economic co-operation. First of all, we have the provinces getting together. Bit by bit we are breaking down the trade barriers which exist between provinces. More important, the problems we have had with international trade, particularly with the United States, are being solved. That conference a week ago in Quebec City was the culmination of a whole series of negotiations which have been going on. Member after Member has criticized the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) with respect to the salmon fishing treaty on the West Coast. We know that he has been around the outports of the West Coast bit by bit, getting advice with respect to the salmon treaty, and we now have an agreement which the previous Government had not been able to reach for years and years.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), would not want to have attributed to her the responsibility for making the salmon treaty which was imposed on the people of British Columbia. It was the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not a point of order.

I am very pleased that we now have recognition that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) has been doing a first-class job. We have the recognition that we have a treaty that they could not organize in a decade. Why not? Because there was no sense of co-operation between Canada and its largest trading partner, the United States of America. We were concerned, and British Columbia was particularly concerned, with respect to the question of softwood lumber. We have already taken virtually one third of the American market for softwood lumber and we were very much in danger of having our lumber exports subjected to countervailing duty. That fear has gone. We were in danger of having our potato exports subject to countervailing duty, and that fear has gone. We were very much in danger of having our steel industry virtually banned from competition in the U.S., and to a large extent that fear has gone.
Members opposite talk about economic confidence. The business community has economic confidence when it sees a Government prepared to get tough and act and to be sensible with respect to trade matters. It is a Government which is prepared to consult. It understands how we must finance export trade. Papers have been produced for discussion with the business community concerning export financing through the banks and other financial institutions. They, too, can then participate the way they should in financing those exports. We will shortly be producing new methods by which the Government will use the financial institutions of this country to develop trade. To say that economic confidence does not exist because somehow a budget has not been produced is just utter drivel. The opposition says that this is not a long time to wait for a budget. Do you realize there was a Government elected
March 25, 1985

on February 18, 1980, and it was not until way on into October of the same year that it finally produced its Budget? Oh, yes, there was an economic statement in April, but we produced an economic statement in November. It is the same type of situation.
We have a situation, Mr. Speaker, where for every dollar we spent in the first 10 months of this fiscal year we took in only 64 cents in taxes. The other 36 cents had to be borrowed. They may well say we are to blame for the management from September 4 until January. But they cannot do that because we have not had a chance to take it over and really get at it. The situation is that the spending is built into programs that were developed five years ago, ten years ago, two years ago and continue to require further funds. They continue to grind away.
Let us look at housing as an example. Under CMHC, and this is but one example, in order to finance new construction of social housing we made loans and guaranteed the interest at 2 per cent. When an apartment building is built and the mortgage is 15 per cent, the subsidy is 13 per cent. But it is not just the subsidy in the year the building is built, it applies the following year, the year after that and the year after that. Virtually all the money set aside in the Estimates for CMHC today are to pay subsidies on buildings built two years ago, five years ago, eight years ago and so on. That will be the situation not next year and the year after but for the next 25 or 30 years. These costs are built in liabilities of the Government of Canada.
So we called together last week the leaders of business, labour, consumer groups, social groups and educational groups from across the country to find out what they thought we might be able to do. To some extent those groups are both the solution and the problem, because many of those people have been involved all the way along in the decision making which has led us to the position we are in. We are criticized for that, but how can you criticize a Government which has enough ability to get Bob White, Dennis McDermott and Louis Laberge in the same room with Rowland Frazee? I say to you, Sir, that that demonstrates our ability to get Canadians working together again.
If we are ever going to solve the economic problems of this country it will be because we get Canadians working together again. The unfortunate situation over the last 15 years is that we have had a Government of confrontation. We have had a Government which has pitted labour against management, management against management, provinces and Territories against provinces, native people against farming groups, farming groups against city dwellers and so on. We have to end that confrontation. We can never build this nation by fighting each other. Heaven knows, we have enough problems as it is in this cold half of North America building a nation in the first place. But to build a nation when you are already deeply in debt, fighting against each other will not help. When Canadians elected us on September 4, they elected us to build together. They did not elect us to do nothing. However, they did not elect us to destroy a fragile recovery through ill-conceived and
Supply
ill-thought-out actions. With regard to farm financing, it would have been very easy to fulfil immediately the promises that we made under Section 31 of the Income Tax Act with respect to capital gains on farm-land and agri-bonds. We could have done that by fiat. However, even farm groups are not in favour of some of those matters. Why would we do them without consulting and without public hearings? Members will know that we have had public hearings. The Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs will be reporting on these matters prior to its mandated requirement of April 1.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will take that report into account in preparing his Budget. Obviously he cannot prepare the Budget without the report. Obviously he cannot do things that will damage our fragile recovery without input from all sectors in the economy and without the understanding of how what is proposed in one sector of the economy affects another sector of the economy.
To say that it is somehow a terrible delay to wait until the week of May 20 is to be a bit naive and a bit ridiculous. We could go ahead and do everything we said we were going to do without consulting, but then it would be complained that we did not consult. We have consulted and we will continue to consult. There are 1.5 million Canadians out of work. There are fewer Canadians out of work today than there were at the time of the election. There will be a lot fewer Canadians out of work as time goes on. It takes a while for business confidence and a new attitude to develop to enable new employment and new job creation to take place. It does not happen overnight.
We have proposed a lessening of controls on foreign investment, but that does not mean that people from abroad will pour their money into our resources. It does not mean that all of a sudden new jobs and opportunities will develop as a result of the change in the statute. However, the change in the statute is a worth-while effort to encourage people to come to Canada and invest in the country.
They say that we have not done anything for small business. We proceeded with the Small Business Loans Act to make it more sensible and to make the banks more responsible for it. That move will enable more funding to be available for small business.
Rome was not built in a day, Mr. Speaker. Our problems of a $35 billion deficit and a $190 billion national accounts debit did not build up overnight. It did not happen just by itself and it is not going to change just because we will it to change. Over the terms of past Governments we have built up a habit of liking a whole lot of government service. However, we do not have the ability to pay for that government service. In our own constituencies we have built up a bad habit of asking the Government for hand-outs.
The other day Domtar came to the country and asked for a hand-out of $100 million. Member after member of the Liberal and New Democratic Parties stood up and demanded that the Government hand over $100 million to Domtar. That is how a great, big national debt is developed. You can only have

March 25, 1985
Supply
the tailor make you a suit with the amount of cloth he has. We have been trying to get too much out of what we have. As responsible Members of Parliament we must realize that. As responsible Members of Parliament we must tell our constituents that rather than looking to government for everything they must do a lot on their own. They must build the country. Co-operatively we can do that.
The Member for Laval-des-Rapides ought to be ashamed of this motion. I appreciate that it is a non-confidence vote. I suppose it would have been easier for the Official Opposition to have merely said, "That this House regrets it has no confidence in the Government" and left it at that. However, he went on to say why he should have confidence in the Government. That being the case, it seems to me that members of the Opposition ought to decry this motion and vote against it, because the motion is a summary of why the House should have confidence in the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I respect him and what he says in the House. I know him quite well and have known him for quite a while. Before his Party was elected he used to talk about how interest rates are too high in the country. He is shaking his head. I can hear him.
You can hear him shake his head?

I can hear him all the way over here. I don't hear very much, only an echo.
He used to make speeches time and again from this part of the House. I simply want to know whether he agrees with the Government's monetary policy. Does he agree with the interest rate policy? I know he is very blunt. If he does not agree, he will tell me, if he does agree, he will also tell me. I know he knows the situation very well. Interest rates are much too high in this country and ordinary Canadians-I guess that is all Canadians except for Jack Horner, in answer to the Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone)-farmers, fishermen, small businessmen and home owners need a made-in-Canada interest rate policy. It must be much lower than it is now. Does the Hon. Member agree that Gerald Bouey should call the shots? Does he agree with the Government's interest rate policy?

Mr. Speaker, I think I should instruct my secretary to make a collection of the speeches I have made in the House on interest rates and to send them to the Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). If he would like, I will discuss them with him so that he will understand how the determination of what interest rates is made. He ought to know that interest rates are a function of the supply and demand for money reflected, to some extent, by the risk a lender takes. On that basis we in this country are paying nearly 2 per cent more than the American Government is paying for its money. That is largely because the public views us as a greater risk. If we did not carry the horrible national debt that we do and if we were running our affairs more sensibly, we would borrow our money considerably cheaper.
If the Governments of Canada and the United States were not sucking up the money from the private savings of their citizens in deficits, money would be considerably cheaper. As the Member for Crowfoot says, there is no such thing as ordinary Canadians. It happens to be a fact that all taxpayers of Canada are paying the interest rates we are paying. The Government of Canada is the largest borrower. The taxpayers of Canada are the largest payers. From looking at the Estimates the Hon. Member will realize that the estimated cost of the national debt this year is in excess of $25 billion. That was calculated on the basis of a supposed interest rate averaging 10.6 per cent. He will know that at the present calculation that figure is wrong and that we will probably have to spend considerably more than $25 billion to carry the outrageous borrowings that we have.
The Hon. Member will also know that interest rates dropped half a point last week. However, that is not good enough. He will know that that is not good enough. I know that is not good enough. The farmers, businessmen, and home owners know that is not good enough. If we had some sensibility in the economy of this country rather than the yapping of the New Democratic Party demanding more, more, more, then we would have lower interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, I think it takes a yapper to recognize one.
Oh, oh!

The Hon. Member is talking about all these people who have savings and so on. I do not know if he recognizes that according to a report in The Globe and Mail recently nine families have half their stocks and bonds in the Toronto Stock Exchange. Since so much wealth is controlled by so few, why would the Hon. Member not agree to bring down interest rates in Canada and, if need be, use foreign exchange controls or an interest equalization tax or something like that for investments of over $50,000 or $60,000 which would affect people who are not ordinary Canadians? There are nine families who control about half the assets on the Toronto Stock Exchange. Why does the Hon. Member stand up for those rich friends of his when we could be doing something for ordinary Canadians?
Never has so much been owned by so many to so few.

I think what the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville would like us to do is to have foreign exchange controls like those in Brazil, Mexico, or Argentina, and then we could also have interest rates like those in Brazil, Mexico, or Argentina. Under that kind of regime which the Hon. Member has in mind, we would be assuring poverty for my children and for my children's children's children, and 1 suppose they would then become ordinary Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) say that the threat against
March 25, 1985

Canadian softwood entering the United States has been removed. If that is the case, could he explain to the House why the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) has gone to Washington today reportedly to deal with that very problem?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will know that the imposition of controls on the importation of softwood lumber has to pass the office of the President of the United States. Obviously, in a way these controls have to go through the House of Representatives and so on. It is important that our Ministers deal directly with legislators and people in the United States having an interest to make sure that as far as possible we ameliorate the problems of the threat of controls.
I say to the Hon. Member that the effect of the Quebec conference was essentially to give us access to the American market, subject to the tariffs but not subject to any unrealistic interference with our trade.

Mr. Speaker, let me raise a question with the Hon. Member. He suggested that there is a problem with exchange controls. Is it not the case that the country his Party now looks to as the exemplary model with respect to economic policy, that is the United States, put into effect an interest equalization tax under a Republican President in the early 1970s which certainly did not destroy confidence in the future of the United States? It had instead the effect of protecting U.S. currency at a time when it was under some pressure.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will know that that tax was immediately abolished because it was not accomplishing anything. He will know that that type of interference in the market-place will not work. More important, the Hon. Member will know that, with the long border we have, with the percentage of our Gross National Product directly involved with foreign trade, particularly foreign trade with the United States, to attempt to isolate and control every foreign exchange transaction that takes place between Canada and the United States would immediately create a disaster in our markets. It would probably immediately put hundreds of thousands of Canadians out of work. If there were an attempt to enforce foreign exchange transactions, it would require an army of policemen to the extent that we would get rid of our unemployment program by putting everybody in uniform.

Mr. Speaker, did this happen in the United States? Were there problems of enforcement or was there not quite a straightforward and simple system whereby the financial institutions reported to the Government? Did it not turn out in the United States to be quite easy to put an interest equalization tax into effect? Would it not be similarly easy here, given that we have a banking system that is quite highly concentrated and on which we could quite easily rely to do the policing involved?

Mr. Speaker, if one thought that one could somehow control the movements of foreign exchange and steer away from the market, I would think that was not the effect of the American equalization tax. It may have intended to be the
Supply
effect, but there were not any demonstrable differences that took place in what would otherwise be the market condition. If you take a look at a market condition where there is an advocacy for some control over foreign exchange to separate our interest rates from interest rates in the United States or world interest rates, the Hon. Member must know as an economist that with the number of transactions going back and forth across the border, and with the number of Canadians who hold large accounts in the United States and of Americans who hold large accounts in Canada, we would soon run into a massive problem.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The period provided for questions and comments has now expired. The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand).

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I want to start by immediately indicating our support for the NDP amendment tabled a few moments ago to add visible minorities and the disabled to the list of those who have been hurt by the lack of action of the present Conservative Government.
Last Thursday we had the eighteenth anniversary of the United Nations Day against Discrimination. On that occasion, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) made a statement. We responded. We made many of the same points that were made a few minutes ago with respect to visible minorities and the handicapped who have suffered a great deal of discrimination not only in employment but in many other areas of this country as well. We support that amendment very strongly.
To return to the motion before us today, Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate my full support and point out that once again by delaying the budget we have also seen a delay of specific action to deal with the unemployed. In addition, the delay has caused a great deal of economic uncertainty among those who would invest in new jobs and those who would wish to make their plans with respect to new plant, equipment, and so on. There is no comparison between the election in 1980 and the election last fall in 1984. The election in 1980 simply returned a Government that had been in power a year previously. It was the same Government. It had already produced budgets before 1980 and it was continuing in the same way. Here we have a new Government that has been almost eight months in office. We have not had a budget. We have had certain policy announcements here and there but the announcements have not been produced in a global way to give us an over-all picture of the Government's economic policy.
These delays are seriously affecting the unemployed, and measures that might be taken by the Government to put the unemployed back to work are affected. I should point out that there has been no delay with respect to cuts. Cuts came rather quickly after the election of September 4. Last November, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced, together with

March 25, 1985
Supply
the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) a whole series of cuts, which not only affected certain government programs but also put a large number of people out of work.
Just last week we had representatives of the cultural community in Ottawa. They were lobbying for the many jobs which were lost and will be lost in the various areas of Canadian culture-symphonies, orchestras, museums, theatre groups, ballet companies and so on. The Government did not wait to introduce these cuts. They acted right away, before they had anything to take their place in many instances. They cut out programs before they really knew what they would put in their place.
Whenever we ask Ministers or other government Members when they will bring in the programs they promised, over and over again they state that they have to wait because they are consulting. "Consulting" has become their favourite word. Of course we agree with consultations. It is a good thing, but it cannot be a replacement or a substitute for action. Many Members on the government side of the House make statements as if consultation was invented on September 4, that there never was any consultation before. I can forgive them because many of them are new Members and were not here before September 4. However, one would think they would read Hansard or be in touch with what happened.
I have a list in my possession which indicates some 12 consultative processes with respect to employment and employment-related matters in the last Parliament alone. One of them 1 had a lot to to with because I was Chairman of the task force on employment opportunities for the '80s. Several Members on the other side worked on that task force as well. We spent two years consulting across the country. We heard from nearly 400 groups and individuals on employment opportunities for the '80s. We published a report which was almost unanimous, except for two or three recommendations on which the Conservatives dissented.
We also had task forces on skills development leave and on major Canadian projects. There was In the Chips, which dealt with the effects of microelectronics on employment. We had the task force on labour market development, the Dodge Commission, the task force on part-time work in Canada, and the Ironside advisory panel. We had the House of Commons Committee on profit sharing in the labour market, the Economic Council report on "In Short Supply", and the Williams task force, on Outreach policy.
It is important to put this list on the record because I am becoming fed up with new Members repeatedly rising and saying that there has never been any consultation. There has been all kinds of consultation. However, there is something important which must follow consultation. This was done in the past, but it has not yet been done by the present Government.
Also, as a result of consultation there was the Economic Council report On the Mend and the Macdonald Commission which went across the country and heard evidence from many
groups from all facets of Canadian life. It has not yet reported. These examples are just in the area of employment.
Also there were task forces on the handicapped, on North-South relations, on a national trading corporation, on alternative energy, on regulatory reform and on pension reform. We had the Technology for Tomorrow Conference, which was much more broadly based than the conference last weekend. We had three major policy forums in 1983 with respect to international affairs, economic policy and employment. I could go on and on, but it should be placed on the record that consultation was not invented on September 4. There was a great deal of consultation during the last Parliament and under the previous Government. However, once consultation takes place, hard decisions have to be made. Sometimes those people with whom one consults will not be pleased because one cannot please everyone. I know the Government is trying to please everyone, but sooner or later when hard decisions are made, some will be alienated and will accuse the Government of not consulting with them.
I am a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I have a lot of respect for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). When he says he consulted, I believe him, but many witnesses have appeared before the committee and have said that he did not consult with them in that the Bill he introduced did not reflect the advice they gave during the consultative process. Whenever a Government brings in highly controversial measures, of course those who are opposed will complain about lack of consultation. However, as I said, the Government is consulting on some things but not at all on others.
I should like to refer to changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act with respect to severance pay which will take place on April 1. The Government did not consult at all. It announced them in the House on November 4 or whatever was the date when the cuts were announced. Now we are receiving petitions and protests from people from all walks of life, including the Armed Forces, labour unions, workers' associations, professional associations and so on. They are asking the Government to delay the implementation of that measure until consultation takes place. They have pointed out some of the implications of that measure which could not have been foreseen when the announcement was made. For example, some people wanted to use severance pay to re-establish themselves in employment or to relocate from one area of the country to another. Some wanted to roll over the money by means of an RSP. Now they will not be able to do these things because the Government has decided that severance pay must be counted as income and that their unemployment insurance will be delayed. The money which they could have used to re-establish themselves in employment or for retirement purposes will have to be used for the necessities of life and consequently will not have the purposes which even the Government had in mind. It would be reasonable for the Government to consult on that one, if it really believes in consultation. It may be possible to
March 25, 1985

modify it in such a way that it will not harm the people I have mentioned.
Consultation is good, as I said, but it has to be followed up with action. Let us hope that we will have action soon. It is unfortunate that the Budget has to be delayed until the week of May 20, as was announced not in the House but at the conference last weekend. We will be continuing to push for some very specific action because the problems will not go away or diminish with wishful thinking.
We try to be as objective and as non-partisan as we can because jobs are important for all Canadians. In all constituencies there are people who voted Conservative, Liberal and NDP. They are not interested in bickering among themselves in the House. They are really interested in something being done to help them find work. However, one has the impression that many of the consultative processes are really media-type politics. The Government is not sure what it wants to do. It tries to bring people together so that it can jump in afterwards, pick up the consensus and lead. Instead of presenting ideas to these groups to discuss, white papers, green papers or whatever, the Government is trying to develop a consensus in the first place. I do not know whether that will work.
We have asked several times for the discussion paper on unemployment insurance, but we have not received it as yet. During the election campaign, as we on this side of the House have mentioned quite often, members of the Government pretended they had the answers. Again I refer to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on July 5 in Prince Albert wherein he said that we would see tens upon tens of thousands of jobs being created just as quickly as the new Government could be sworn in.
He said that?

Yes, he did. He made similar statements on several occasions. One would have thought, in listening to that statement during the election campaign, that the Prime Minister and the Conservative Party had done their consultation during the many years they were in opposition and when they had the time to consult with many groups. They gave the impression, wrongly, that they had plans for action with which they were ready to proceed immediately after the election, and of course they did not.
I do not fault them for admitting now that these problems, the problems of economic growth, or interest rates are complex matters because they are complex. We always stated that they were complex matters, despite the fact we were trying to act and produce jobs. We were not always as successful as we wished. Nevertheless, when we tried to explain the difficulties we were up against, they denigrated our answers. They ridiculed the answers and deceived the Canadian people into believing that they in fact had pat solutions, that they had the answers. It is for that that I criticize them, that deceit they practised during the election, not for the seriousness of many of their Ministers looking now for solutions. For those honestly
Supply
looking for solutions, I congratulate them, but for that deceit that they perpetrated on the Canadian people during the election campaign I find them greatly at fault. They will have to answer for that.
What have they done with respect to employment since the election? In addition to making a lot of severe cuts in the Department of Employment and other Departments, which led to a loss of jobs, they cancelled the First Choice program which would have put 100,000 young Canadians into jobs, giving them some experience at employment. They replaced it with a much smaller program called the Youth Training Option, a much smaller sort of trial project.
Let us look at the number of jobs created. When my party was in Government, I was often critical of them because they did not do more. The record shows that in 1978, 334,000 jobs were created; in 1979, 410,000 new jobs were created; in 1980, there were 314,000. In 1981, going into the recession, there were 297,000 new jobs. In the recovery year, 1983, more than
400,000	new jobs were created at a time when there was a great growth in our labour force. In that year, our labour force grew 58 per cent faster than the labour force in the United States. Despite the fact that 400,000 new jobs were created, the rate of unemployment remained pretty much the same because of this increase in the labour force.
In 1984, a year that was shared by both Parties in government, there were 250,000 jobs created in Canada up to the last count. In the second quarter, there were 108,000 jobs, in the third quarter, 67,000 jobs and in the fourth quarter 88,000 jobs created. There has been no dramatic increase in employment as a result of the Conservatives taking power, contrary to what they would have us believe before the election. In addition, they have not put before the Canadian people a plan that would lead to the creation of such jobs.
In answer to some of our questions about their cutting out programs, their answer has been that they do not believe you can solve the problem of unemployment by throwing money at problems, that you do not solve the problem by the Government continually intervening. Some of them believe that if the Government withdraws in certain key areas, the private sector will have confidence and create those jobs. So far, there has been no real indication that that is taking place. This is due to the fact that there has been no budget until now.
The private sector is not really certain in which direction it is going to go. It is quite plain that we have two parties within the Conservative Party. We have the Conservative ideologues, those who believe in the philosophy I just expressed, that if the Government withdraws, the private sector will produce. I do not support that. There are some people who believe very strongly in that, including some economists. A good number of people in the Conservative caucus and in Government believe in that.
On the other hand, there are the pragmatists who are attempting to run the Government by means of polls: whatever pleases they will do. We saw examples of that in the first six months that they were in power. First we had announcements with respect to the cuts in social programs or the changes in

March 25, 1985
Supply
social programs that would lead to a lack of universality. After a great deal of debate in this House and in the country, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) announced that there would not be such cuts in old age pensions and in family allowances and that they would approach it in a different way. That kind of "first we are this way" and "then we are that way" is not producing the confidence that is expected.
1 repeat, it is essential for this Parliament and for the people of the country to know the over-all global approach of that new Government to the economy so that all of us can then debate it in a proper way. Those of us who agree with it can support it. Those who wish to oppose it will oppose it. The private sector of the country and the voluntary sector, the trade unions and so on, can make their plans accordingly. They have 211 people supporting them. I suppose if they want to do something, they are going to do it, no matter what we do in this House. We will try to influence public opinion in this debate, but we know that we are not going to win too many votes.
The record can be checked. There has been no significant change so far. Canadians are still waiting. What can be done and what should be done with respect to employment? Again I am going to repeat what I heard in nearly two years of hearings across this country. I see, Mr. Speaker, you are indicating that my time is almost up. I guess I had better sum it up.
When a Government or Parliament decides that it is going to do something, that it is going to make that its highest priority, it can do it if it has the political will. The previous Government did it with six and five. I did not agree with every way with which we approached six and five, but we were at 12 to 13 per cent inflation. The Government made up its mind that it would make that its highest priority and bring inflation down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent over a three-year period. It happened. Of course it happened. There were other influences that were in there. The Government made it its highest priority. It made six and five the rallying cry in this country. It worked. Inflation came down, and it is still down.
My final word is, let us do the same with employment. Let us have a six and five for employment. Let us put our political will behind it. It will have the support of a lot of Members of this House. Let us bring down the unemployment rate to six and five and let us do it soon.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions and comments?
[ Translation]
The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), for questions or comments.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member whether he believes the weekend economic conference-and I know the Hon. Member has had some experience as a member of Cabinet in the past-would have been more successful if the Government had tabled draft solutions or a
white paper or departmental papers which would have served as points of discussion for conference participants and on which an attempt could have been made to reach a consensus. The Hon. Member may recall that this was tried in Australia-in fact, the Prime Minister of Australia was in Ottawa-when the Australian Government tabled documents at a consultation conference, indicating the direction it wanted to give this country from the economic and social point of view, and this did bring results. This time, however, we had no such government paper. Does the Hon. Member believe the results would have been better if the Government had given some direction?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I believe it would have helped and would have led to more significant results because it would have focused the convention on the proposal of the Government rather than leaving it as wide open as it did. I know the Government asked the delegates to the convention to discuss the problems of unemployment and economic growth, investment and so on. However, it would have focused it still more and led to more concrete results if it had put its own working paper, whether it was a white paper or whatever you call it, before that conference.
In doing that you run a risk because you are taking a stand. I can recall the previous Government saying that it was putting some proposals before the country for consultation and they are still identified with them to a certain extent. As far as I am concerned, the nature of politics is the taking of tough and difficult stands. I know the Government will be howled at, picketed and voted against from time to time. However, I think that would have led to a more productive conference.
The one thing of which the delegates were aware was the November statement of the Minister of Finance and his promise that there would be more of the same in the next Budget. They had an inkling as to what line the Government would take. It appears as though, despite the fact that there was a division of opinion as to whether the highest priority should be cutting back the deficit or solving the unemployment problem, if the newspaper reports are correct, the Minister of Finance still intends to proceed in the same way as he was intending to proceed when he entered the conference. He said that there may be some minor changes considered in the Budget, but basically his over-all approach will be more or less what he was thinking of previously. We do not know exactly what that is yet because we do not know what the Budget will contain. If it is a follow-up on the November economic statement and if it is to be as harsh as the Prime Minister warned it would be when he said that there would be some tough medicine to swallow, that is not the right way to proceed.
Getting together with labour, management and the voluntary groups is always a good thing. However, it could have been done in a better way and it could have been done in a way that would have led to action faster than a Budget in May.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member was on this side of the House for some 14 or 15 years, part of which time he was a Minister of the Crown. Can he tell me when the Government led by the former Prime Minister was able to get the labour leaders, the bankers, the social leaders and the leaders of the private sector together in one conference to discuss issues over one weekend? Can he remember that kind of consultation taking place? Does he not think that that is a pretty fair way to begin building together as Canadians to make this country grow again?

Mr. Speaker, I referred to the conference that was called on October 18, 1982, by the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) who was then, I believe, President of the Treasury Board. The conference was called Technology for Tomorrow. It dealt with a more concentrated subject, the very serious impact of new technology on employment, and it was similar in nature to the national economic conference. It was a summit conference held on a weekend and included representatives from all sectors. I cannot recall if there were more representatives at that conference than at this one.
As well, there were three major policy forums held in northern Quebec by the Government in the summer of 1983. Those forums went on for two or three days and included spokesmen from business, labour and international backgrounds. The wheel vis-a-vis consultation was not invented on September 4.
As I mentioned in my remarks, following these consultations, the Government took action. In some cases, the public agreed with its action and in some cases it did not agree. I suppose that is the nature of politics and the nature of making hard decisions. We run a risk when doing certain things but at least, if we believe in them and believe that that is the way things should be done, we should proceed.
On occasion, I have been critical of the present Government and have thought that there should be even more consultation. I am still critical of the Government. I mentioned the example of the Government proceeding with cuts to the unemployment insurance regarding severance pay without consulting. I wish that there had been consultation on that matter. However, it does not have to be drawn out forever and a day.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member agrees that we should have consultation. Mr. Speaker, I trust that the fact that Hon. Members opposite who proposed this motion took off early for the weekend is not an indication of how seriously they regard these important issues. They raised these issues in the amendment which we take very seriously indeed.
I would like to point out that the motion claiming that the timing proposed for the Budget means that the Government has taken no concrete action to create jobs and establish economic confidence among Canadians including the groups mentioned in the amendment today is among the most absolutely absurd allegations I have heard since I entered this Chamber. It flies in the face of the record of action taken by the Government.
I would like to review some of the highlights of our accomplishments, but first I want to remind Hon. Members across the way that this Government is governing our great country differently. Canadians from across the country are saying amen to that. They realize, as we do, that the well trodden paths from years before lead nowhere. It is our job, as they know and we know, to blaze new trails of governing in this country.
For the first time in Canadian history, Canadians from all walks of life, including the disabled, women's groups, natives' groups, labour, business and community volunteers met together with each other and with the Government at the same time. This Government, unlike the former Government, is not afraid to meet Canadians face to face. It is not afraid to meet Canadians with disparate interests but with a common objec-

tive, the objective of building a better future for this great country.
Consensus has not been reached in everything. We do not expect unanimity. What the Government desires is a more comprehensive understanding among the very groups to which we have referred. The national economic conference led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was more than a meeting of minds; it was exciting and it was historic. It was a concrete example of our respect for the opinions of Canadians across the country and of our desire to involve Canadians in the policies which affect them. I want to remind, particularly Hon. Members opposite, of something in which this Government believes very strongly-that democracy is based on the conviction that there are extraordinary possibilities in ordinary people.
I would like to review what the Government has accomplished and what Members opposite have chosen to ignore. Within three days of the opening of the new Parliament, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) presented to the House an extensive economic and fiscal statement on November 8. That agenda for economic renewal charted the most comprehensive overhaul of economic policies ever undertaken by a national Government. We have taken on an enormous challenge which will require the full concentration and co-operation of the people of Canada in every sector, people of good will as well as those in Government. By definition, it is a job which will take years, not just months. It is a job which is already well started.
I would like to illustrate the wide range a concrete actions which have already been taken. The November statement announced a total of $4.2 billion in expenditure reductions and revenue recovery measures to be implemented in fiscal year 1985-86. It declared the longer-range goal of reducing the projected level of annual expenditure by 1990 by between $10 billion and $ 15 billion. It was a long-awaited start to reducing the federal deficit. It was a start on putting the Government's fiscal house in order. The statement was a recognition that the mounting federal debt had become a powerful obstacle to growth and to private sector job creation. Whatever consensus may not have been reached, there is consensus on that. The start on deficit reduction was an essential step toward rebuilding confidence.
The Minister took action on social policy, within the limits of the Government's difficult financial position, to improve support for Canadians who need and deserve assistance. The spousal allowance program was extended to all widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64. That measure will benefit some 85,000 low-income Canadians, mostly women, starting in the fall of this year.
The statement also announced improvements in veterans' pensions to ensure more generous and equitable treatment to veterans with disabilities. Those veterans were ignored by the former Government.
On the employment front, the Minister of Finance, in the November statement, committed an additional $1 billion in
the coming fiscal year to help Canadians acquire new skills and find jobs in the private and public sectors. It will provide more effective delivery of employment and training programs. Among those benefiting are the disabled. The best thing we can do for the disabled is to turn them into taxpayers so that they share in the prosperity along with the rest of us.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) announced detailed measures to implement that policy through the Challenge '85 summer employment program and the over-all training and employment strategy.
The statement also announced that the Foreign Investment Review Agency would be replaced by Investment Canada, with a new mandate to promote economic development in Canada. It signalled major changes to the so-called Crown interests, or back-in provisions, of the National Energy Program.
To resolve taxpayer uncertainty, the Minister of Finance took action to clear up a number of outstanding tax issues dating as far back as 1982. He carried out this Party's undertaking that, in a dispute between a taxpayer and Revenue Canada, the taxpayer will be considered innocent until a judge has ruled otherwise, despite the ruthless policies of the former Government in this area.
The November statement announced assistance to the resource industries-to farmers, fishermen, loggers and mine operators. Two modifications were made to the changes in the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax which were proposed by the former Government. A one-year extension was provided for the lower rate of PGRT applying to integrated oil sands projects. That is a benefit to the West which was beleaguered by the former Government's policies. As well, it increased the threshold levels of the small producers' credit under the PGRT to $500,000.
Another step which was taken was the appointment of the task force under the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) to review federal programs and regulations, consolidate, simplify, end duplication and improve service to the public in an area which had atrophied for years and years under the former Government.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced a reduction in interest rates on Farm Credit Corporation loans. He introduced legislation to establish a price stabilization program for red meat producers, and to allow the establishment of a supply-management program for tobacco growers.
The railway passenger service received a vote of confidence by the decision of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankow-ski) to reinstate three VIA Rail services in the Maritimes, Ontario and western Canada. Those services were eliminated by the former Government, despite the protests of the people who were affected.
Economic regional development agreements were signed with Quebec, British Columbia, and Ontario. ERDA subagreements were signed on a whole range of sectoral development plans, including pulp and paper, tourism, fisheries, indus-

trial development, communications, development planning, and science and technology, right across the country.
A major provincial agreement, resolving years of controversy, which will open up new hope for economic growth in Newfoundland was the agreement signed on offshore resource development with that province by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney). Believe me, we on this side of the House are very proud of our colleague and the Atlantic Accord.
Hear, hear!

Perhaps, the most fundamental change, and one which is welcomed across the country, is the new approach to consultation and co-operation with Canadians in all walks of life in planning the federal policies which 1 mentioned at the outset of my remarks. The Agenda Paper was a statement of national purpose and the focus for subsequent consultations with all sectors of the Canadian community. It signalled the Government's intention to clear away obstacles to growth and to release the creative energies of Canadians to build a better future. The paper recognized the important economic responsibilities of the provincial Governments. The consultation of the Prime Minister with the Premiers of the ten provinces in Regina set a new standard in effective co-operation in the national interests. Again, that positive approach was repeated in the highly successful national economic conference which ended on Saturday. Those of us who were there, and those who watched it across the country, sensed the excitement of that conference.
In our relationship with our neighbours, two meetings have been held between the Prime Minister and the President of the United States. Those meetings resulted in vital agreements on trade relations, acid, rain, northern defence and Pacific salmon.
The last four months have seen a series of consultation papers focusing on particular areas of our economic life. They have dealt with access to export markets, which is the lifeblood of Canada; export financing, which is required to support that trade; small business development; mining; benefits for children and the elderly; housing; job training; and tax issues in agriculture. Some of the papers focus on practical ways in which business and Government can plan and work together to build a stronger economy and create jobs. Others examine ways of ensuring that our social support system is sensitive to those who most need help. All of the papers recognize not only the vital need for action, but the need for a full opportunity for Canadians to contribute to major policy decisions.
There is more I could say, but the point is that this Government has acted, and it has acted quickly, in a great many concrete ways. The Government has initiated a concentrated national effort to involve Canadians so that they can sense how the Government is trying to build the future in order that they can help it with that. Our actions, and the process of discussion and debate which we have initiated, are contributing directly to the restoration of confidence in the future of the country. The quickness of Members opposite to belittle the

actions of this Government is one thing-wearisome, but predictable-but the cavalier disregard which is shown in this motion and the amendment for the contributions which Canadians can make to the forthcoming Budget is the real indicator of the cynical and worn-out approach that characterizes the group across the way. They are out of touch, Mr. Speaker, and out of sync with the people of this country. No wonder Canadians overwhelmingly rejected them last September 4, and they do not yet realize that some pretty important changes were made on that day. Not only did the Government change but the way in which the Government works changed. It changed for the better. We now have a truly national Government which wants to work with and listen to Canadians in every part of the public and private sector and in every part of Canada. This takes time and is crucial to the sense of responsibility which Canadians expect from us, the Government they elected. The sooner this new reality sinks in over on the other side of the House, Mr. Speaker, the sooner Hon. Members opposite can begin to contribute in a constructive way in meeting Canada's economic challenges.
Let those Hon. Members also recognize that the economy is showing real signs of encouragement now and for the future, for the unemployed, in particular. Jobs are being created, growth has been higher than expected, the trade balance continues at record levels, inflation is under good control, our competition position is strengthening, and confidence is on the upswing.
We have the momentum going in this country and that was communicated to us by the people who attended our conference this weekend. We intend to build on that momentum in the forthcoming Budget. We are going to keep on building in the months and years after that. There is a big job to be done, Mr. Speaker, and it will be done best with the co-operation and support of all Hon. Members of this House. But it will be done regardless, and done well with the help of people from every part of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to comment. Mr. Speaker, I am always struck by how magnificently this Minister speaks to us. She puts up a grand and spirited defence of the indefensible.
I have three specific questions which I would like to raise with the Minister coming out of this weekend. I was an observer at the national economic conference. First, if there was a sense in Government that eight weeks was needed between the national economic conference and the Budget, why was the Budget originally scheduled for the end of April? The Government itself set up the original schedule with the sense that a month would be sufficient to take into account the points raised this past weekend.
Second, I have to raise specifically with the Minister what to me, and I think to a great many of the people who were there, was the most dramatic event of the weekend. That was the fact that 81 people out of 136 signed a petition to ask for a specific change on a specific damaging and mean-spirited piece of government initiative, that is to include severance pay in calculations of unemployment insurance benefits. That is something, incidentally, which the President of Alcan-who is not exactly as wild a radical as my friend from Nickel Belt- stressed should not only not be considered as part of unemployment insurance calculations but should not even be taxed so that severance pay could be put into small businesses. Why is the Government, to show its good faith, not prepared to
accept that very simple suggestion in responding to that conference and back down on severance pay?
Third, would the Minister not agree that there have been incredibly mixed signals with respect to whether deficit cutting or job expansion is to be stressed, whether free trade is the policy, as the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) seems to suggest, or whether it is the view of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), who seems to talk in terms of increased protectionism, that is the policy? The mixed signals seem to me to be very extensive. Surely the Minister would agree, from her own background in financial circles, that such mixed signals to the financial community are in fact creating uncertainty which must be resolved before the business community in this country can start to undertake the investments which I think all of us would like to see move ahead?

Mr. Speaker, I think that the consultations which are leading up to the Budget have been enormously significant and successful. We expected them to be successful. They have been more successful than we expected. Canadians do have something to say to us concerning what we are doing. I want to say something else about the date of the Budget, and that is that unlike the former Government, when we bring down our Budget we intend to bring it in at a time when we can do it right.
In connection with the severance pay issue, my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, was at the conference. I know the solutions that she will come up with will be fair and reasonable after taking consultation into account. However, I might point out that the highlight, the most exciting part of the conference, was not the signing of the petition, it was watching people dialogue together. It was hearing the head of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women say that she had never realized before the complexities the Government faces in trying to bring various interests together. That was the most exciting part of the conference.
In answer to the third question, there are no mixed signals. There was a discussion on the deficit and job creation. There is a greater realization in this country than ever before that the two are related, and we are moving on both fronts as rapidly as we can. But the difficulty in balancing those two was something that people who were at that conference realized more than ever after the weekend.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Hon. Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) this afternoon when she was telling us about the Government reducing the Farm Credit Corporation's interest rate to 12.75 per cent. What she did not mention was that last week the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) increased the rate to 13.5 per cent. I wonder if the notes the Minister was speaking from this afternoon were prepared before the Minister of Agriculture increased those rates. This increase was totally uncalled for. If you look at the agricultural community today and the tremendous trials and tribulations they are facing in many parts of the country, that the Government should have increased interest rates for farm loans at this time is totally indefensible. I just wondered whether the Minister of Agriculture bothered to tell the Minister of State for Finance that he was increasing those rates. I thought those matters had to be cleared with the Department of Finance and I am surprised she was not aware of that.
1 was also interested in her comment regarding what this Government is doing for science and technology. I wondered whether she had really taken time to read carefully what the

Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) did on November 8 when he cut some $5 million or $6 million from the toxicology centre at the University of Guelph. That surely had to be one of the most serious blows to that particular part of the scientific field. I know the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard) is in the Chamber this afternoon. I know he would not have agreed with such a decision because he is a former President of the University of Guelph and he knows what a model project that was. That is not because it was a federal project, because it was not just a federal project. There was another $8 million from the private sector. It would have established a world class centre, not only for studying and developing techniques to deal with the difficult problem of toxic elements in our environment, but also for training scientists to deal with these problems. We would have had a world class institution at a very reasonable cost. The institution would have been jointly sponsored by the University of Toronto and the University of Guelph, two world class universities. One has a great deal of expertise in agriculture and veterinary medicine, and the other a great deal of expertise, knowledge and knowhow in the field of human medicine. When the Minister talks about what is being done by this Government, I hope she will think about that decision, which surely had to be one of the worst decisions this Government has taken. We have read about the Love Canal. We read stories about toxins in our environment. We read about the chemicals and pesticides being used in our forest and farms. Everyone is concerned about the question of whether the substances are the cause of cancer or other diseases both in livestock and in people. So I think the Government should not be very proud of its record in science and technology.
I am also amazed that the Minister should have raised the question of extending the spousal allowance to all widows and widowers whether or not they had ever been married to a person receiving the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement. The hue and cry in my part of the country is, how can the Government be so unfair? How can it not provide this to people who have never been married and to people who have been divorced or separated? The Government talks about fairness. It gets caught up in this rhetoric of fairness, but it does not recognize the unfairness of that provision. I receive petitions and letters asking why the Government does not provide that spousal allowance to all people between 60 and 65 years of age irrespective of whether they are widows or widowers. We commend the Government for extending it that far, but why does it not extend it as well to people who have never been married or have been separated or divorced?

I tell the people that 1 do not know. The Government puts out white papers on social security problems. It puts out policies on tourism and all kinds of things. Government Members run around the country asking what they should do about old age pension and other issues. However, they do not get down to the systematic work of implementing all the promises they made.
The Minister spent quite a bit of time talking about implementing the last tax Bill of Mr. Lalonde. I thought that was very interesting. She told the House that they were going to simplify the tax system for small business. These are all good Liberal policies and I was glad she mentioned that. She talked about the benefits provided for RRSP roll-overs, which was also in Mr. Lalonde's Budget. That was very interesting. I was amazed that she mentioned the white paper issued by the Minister of Finance on the farm taxation issues. The Hon. Minister is from the City of Toronto and therefore probably does not hear a lot of the flak that we in rural areas hear about tax issues in agriculture. This is certainly becoming one of the best sellers in rural Canada because, with the name of the Minister of Finance on it, it is clearly the policy of the Government of Canada.
If one reads this document it is clear that the Minsiter of Finance thinks that farmers earn twice as much as the average Canadian, pay a quarter as much taxes, and are worth eight times as much as the average Canadian. This document, published by the Minister of Finance in January of this year, is very much opposed to the 338 promises made by the Government. This paper is opposed to providing low interest longterm financing through agri-bonds. This white paper is clearly opposed to making changes in Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. It is clearly opposed to providing tax free capital gains for farmers. Yet that is what the Government said it was going to do. I am at a loss to know why the Minister of State for Finance would mention this paper which is clearly opposed to all of the things that the agricultural community of the country wants.
Headlines and reports in farm papers have shown that the Minister of Finance is very much opposed to helping farmers at this time. In The Globe and Mail Report on Business of March 7 a headline reads, "Wilson Backtracks of Farm Aid". On page 1 and 2 of The Globe and Mail of February 23, 1985, the headline reads, "Study Shows Farmers Earn Twice as Much as the Average Canadian". The article goes on to say that the average farmer only pays one-quarter as much in taxes. These are statements by the Minister of Finance in his farm review paper. Another headline in the Ottawa Citizen of
Tuesday, February 26, reads, "Western Farmers Enraged by Federal Study on Income". A heading in the Montreal Gazette in January reads, "Farm Paper Ignores Tory Promises". It goes on to outline how the paper talks down why the Government should keep its campaign commitments. Another article in the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of February 28, reads, "Oxford Farm Group Demand Apology From The Finance Chief'. There is no mention in this paper about the Tory campaign promises.
The amazing part of this document issued by the Minister of Finance is not only that it demonstrates his ignorance about the difficulties that agriculture is facing today, but that the Minister of Finance has completely ignored the fact that the farm debt crisis in certain sectors of the industry is the worst it has been since the 1930s. A report issued by the Farm Credit Corporation on October 30, 1984 on the farming situation across the country indicated that 17 per cent of Canadian farmers are experiencing severe financial difficulty and another 7 per cent are in moderate financial distress. This report indicates that 12 per cent of farmers in Atlantic Canada and 20 per cent in British Columbia are facing severe financial distress. All in all, Mr. Speaker, it is pretty serious situation. Some 39,000 farmers are experiencing serious financial distress. That does not mean that they cannot afford to buy a new pick-up truck.
The Farm Credit Corporation used three criteria. The first was that the equity of an individual on his farm was less than 15 per cent. Anyone with less equity than that is in serious financial difficulty. The second criterion was that the borrowings are 110 per cent above the investment. In other words, the person is living on borrowed money. The third criterion is that more than 40 per cent of the farm sales are being used to service intermediate and long-term debt.
When the Minister of Finance reports that the average farmer is so much better off, he is comparing a farmer with an investment of $400,000 or $500,000 with the average home owner and the return on investment. That is pretty silly. Most people would not even think of that kind of comparison. One is a business person with a capital investment averaging about $500,000 of which the equity is about $400,000 and the debt about $100,000 across the entire country. To compare that with the average home owner with a $47,000 home is like comparing two things that are not in the same ballpark. If you compare small business investment and net worth with the farmer, then you have comparable groups, although even there you would have a wider variation. Clearly this is a very unfair paper. It does not do justice nor is it fair to the farmers of Canada. That is why the resolution today regrets that the Government is putting off a Budget until sometime in late May and regrets that the Government does not provide economic confidence for the realization of the hopes of our farmers.
It seems to me that nobody can question a long-term delay of the Budget, and not knowing exactly what the Government

is going to do is causing a great deal of concern. Consultation is fine, but the Government has certain financial commitments. It has certain promises that it made in the election campaign. I think Canadians want to know which ones will be honoured. We know pretty well from the economic statement last fall which ones will not be honoured. We know all kinds of things that were not mentioned in the election campaign which the Tories are not going to do. We know what the Government is opposed to. We know the Tories are opposed to the toxicology centre at the University of Guelph. We know the Tories are opposed to the Canadian Wildlife Service and to the control of the monitoring of the environment in the Great Lakes. We have a whole list of issues such as that of renewable energy and all of those issues that we know the Tories are opposed to. What we do not know is what the Government is in favour of. We could find that out if the Government were to bring forth a Budget. We think the Government should be doing that and that it should not be putting off bringing down a Budget for another two months.

Mr. Speaker, it is very sad to hear the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) say that we do not know what we are for with respect to the agricultural industry. In the seven months that we have been in Government, 57 initiatives have been taken by us that are beneficial to the agricultural community. I dare him to lay on my desk in 24 hours 57 initiatives that were taken by the former Minister of Agriculture in the ten years that the Hon. Gene Whelan held that portfolio. I doubt very much that the Hon. Member could begin to demonstrate the kind of positive action that has been taken in the agricultural community by us. It was the Liberal Government that set forward a grain transportation policy that had the rates going up and up and up, and then a review committee came along to analyse whether the rates should go up. We came into power and we froze the rates. I would like to know why the Member thinks that the Liberals should be applauded for such action.
Once the quotas were met on Irish beef, the Liberals continued to leave the gate open and allowed a flood. Why is the Member standing in his place today pretending such a policy which the Liberals imposed on the agricultural community in Canada was satisfactory? The Hon. Member should know that the present Government has reduced gas tax to farmers, that there have been changes to the Western Grain Stabilization Act, that there has been a pay-out and another pay-out is coming this spring, that interest rates with the FCC have been decreased by approximately 2 per cent, that the tobacco growers have had an opportunity for a new system for marketing which they asked for, and that there is a Bill of Rights for taxpayers that has important implications for farmers. The list goes on until we reach No. 57.
I challenge and I dare the Hon. Member to give me a list of 57 initiatives by the Liberals over the last 10 years.

The Minister of Agriculture in his more unguarded moments has said that the Tories are not going to do anything about it. That is another reason we would like to see a Budget to confirm to the 39,000 farmers looking for some relief and some assistance that the Government will not do anything to provide relief.

After Ireland dumped some 51 million pounds during the latter half of 1984, the Government finally, after four months in office, invoked the meat import law and restricted-I hear the Hon. Member across the way. Let me say to him it is because we never had the volumes over the minimum rate. If he knew what was going on with the whole Irish beef question, he would not be raising it. over by one million pounds. Does that sound like a Government that has any guts, a Government that will protect the beef producers here, Mr. Speaker? It sure does not, because the Tories are in Brussels today negotiating to increase the amount. The EEC is demanding an increase from 6 million pounds to 33 million pounds. There is every likelihood that the Tories will knuckle under. The Hon. Member asks why. Because the Tories have already knuckled under in response to American pressure. The Government has increased the quota to the Americans from 21 million pounds to some 65 million pounds. It does not sound to me as if the Government were very committed to livestock and beef producers of the country or to protecting their interests. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few remarks at the end of this debate. In listening to the debate today, it seemed to me that far too much attention was focused on the conference which took place last weekend in Ottawa. In the long run I suspect that that conference will not have that much impact upon the unemployed logger, miner, factory worker or the young person coming out of college and looking for a job in a market where there are no jobs.
The motion before us is an important one. We are faced with a situation where there are two conflicting tendencies which are on a collision course. On the one hand, new technologies mean that fewer people are needed to perform the work required, so people become redundant. For example, in British Columbia the forest industry can have record production with 20 per cent fewer workers. On the other hand, we see a great many cut-backs in the kinds of services available to people. This means that jobs become more important than ever. They are the only ticket for people who want to get into the banquet which society provides. If people do not have jobs, they are locked out.
We see this in the increased use of user fees and increased premiums for medicare. Many people in Canada are simply not making adequate use of medical facilities because they cannot afford the premiums or user fees. Jobs become more important than ever in this context.
1 should like to make a few comments about the situation facing our aboriginal people. We have often heard the statistic that up to 90 per cent of people in some Indian communities are unemployed. This statistic is becoming more relevant all the time. A few years ago many of these communities had local economies and the people were able to sustain themselves from the land. These economies are being destroyed by massive development. Just a few weeks ago I visited the Lubicon people in northern Alberta. Until five years ago only 10 per cent of those people were on welfare. Today, 90 per cent of them are on welfare because the oil industry criss-crossed their traditional hunting and trapping grounds, destroying their
traditional economy. Now these people find they have no recourse but to go on welfare, which is unable to sustain them as a people. It might put a little bread on their table, but it does not enable them to live as a community. For this reason the World Council of Churches referred to the Lubicon and said that the practices there were in fact genocidal.
It is of the utmost importance that the federal Government take the lead in recognizing the need for the entrenchment of the right of aboriginal people to self-government and to provide adequate resources so that they can govern themselves and have control over their own economy and society.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) referred to the NDP action task force on jobs. I want to focus on one comment which he made. He said there was a greater need for putting resources at the local level so that people had local control. This is what we have been saying with regard to Indian people, but it is also true in hundreds of communities across Canada. It makes good economic sense. If local people have control of the resources, they will make better use of them.
Finally, if the Government has any plans to alleviate the situation for unemployed Canadians, why does it not bring them in now? Why does it have to wait until the end of May? The Government has been in power since September 4. Let it take action now and do what it can to provide some real help for women, young people, natives, fishermen, loggers, and other people of Canada who desperately need that help.
